scenarios.title: The demo that isn't a product
scenarios.situation: A team demos a chatbot that answers questions brilliantly on the founder's laptop. In production it hallucinates on edge cases, costs $4 per conversation, and has no logging of what it told users.
scenarios.prompt: What separates the demo from a production AI system?
choices: Production requires the systems disciplines the demo skipped: evaluation on representative data (not vibes), cost/latency budgets per request, logging and traceability of outputs, guardrails for edge cases, and monitoring for drift — the model is one component; the system is the product.
A bigger model: demos fail in production only because the model is too small.
More prompt engineering: the demo prompt just needs to be longer.
Nothing: demos and production systems are identical; the users are wrong.
scenarios.why: The model is the engine; the product is the car. Evaluation, cost control, observability, and guardrails are what make an AI system shippable — none of them live inside the weights.
scenarios.hint: What did the laptop demo never have to survive?

scenarios.title: Leakage in the pipeline
scenarios.situation: A classifier scores 99% accuracy in testing but 61% in production. Investigation finds the training data included a column ('support_ticket_id') that is only populated AFTER the outcome the model predicts.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what is the fix?
evidence: Target leakage happens when training features contain information unavailable at prediction time — the model learns to read the answer key, not the problem. Test accuracy is then a fiction; production, where the leak is absent, reveals the true (poor) performance.
choices: Target leakage: the ticket ID is a post-outcome artifact, so the model learned the label's shadow — fix by enforcing a temporal feature cutoff (only data available at prediction time may be features) and re-validating with time-split evaluation.
The model is underfit; add more layers until test accuracy returns.
Production data is corrupted; the 99% test score is the true performance.
The fix is to include even more post-outcome columns to raise production accuracy.
scenarios.why: Leakage is time travel in the training set: features from the future make the past look predictable. The defense is a strict temporal cutoff — features may only use information the production system will actually have.
scenarios.hint: What did the model know in training that it cannot know in production?

scenarios.title: RAG or fine-tune?
scenarios.situation: A team needs a support bot over 10,000 company docs that change weekly. One engineer proposes fine-tuning the model on the docs monthly; another proposes retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over a vector index updated daily.
scenarios.prompt: Which approach fits, and why?
evidence: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in retrieved documents at query time — fresh knowledge without retraining, with citations. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights — better for style/behavior, but stale the day after training and expensive to repeat. The choice follows the knowledge's change rate.
choices: RAG: the docs change weekly, so query-time retrieval over a daily-updated index keeps answers fresh with citations — monthly fine-tuning would serve stale knowledge most of the time and pay retraining costs for a problem retrieval solves.
Fine-tuning: baked-in knowledge is always more accurate than retrieval.
Neither: the team should memorize the docs and answer manually.
Both simultaneously: fine-tune daily and also run RAG, regardless of cost.
scenarios.why: Match the mechanism to the knowledge lifecycle: fast-changing facts belong in retrieval (updated daily, cited per answer); stable behavior and style belong in fine-tuning. Weekly-changing docs are a retrieval problem.
scenarios.hint: How fast does the knowledge change, and what does each method cost to refresh?

scenarios.title: The metric that lied
scenarios.situation: A fraud model's precision is 98%, celebrated in a launch review. A month later, investigators find it catches only 12% of actual fraud — the business bleeds while the metric glows.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and which metric should have led?
evidence: Precision = of flagged items, how many were truly fraud. Recall = of all actual fraud, how much was caught. High precision with low recall means the model is conservative: rarely wrong when it fires, but silent on most fraud. The business needed recall (catch the fraud), possibly at some precision cost.
choices: Metric mismatch: precision measured the model's caution, but the business needed recall — catching fraud. The launch should have been gated on recall (and its cost trade-off), with precision as a secondary constraint, because missed fraud is the expensive error here.
The model is fine; 98% precision means fraud is solved and investigators are mistaken.
Precision and recall are the same thing; the team misread the dashboard.
The fix is to stop measuring; metrics cause Goodhart problems.
scenarios.why: Metrics are objectives in disguise: optimize precision and you get a timid model. Choose the metric that prices the business's actual error costs — here, missing fraud dwarfs false alarms — and gate launches on it.
scenarios.hint: Which error is expensive here: the false alarm, or the missed fraud?

scenarios.title: The drifting model
scenarios.situation: A credit-risk model's approval rate for a demographic segment shifts 18% over two quarters with no code changes. The team debates whether this is 'just the market' or a model problem.
scenarios.prompt: How should they investigate, in order?
choices: Follow the monitoring runbook: first check input distribution drift (feature stats vs. training baseline) and label/pipeline integrity (did an upstream schema change?), then segment performance (is accuracy degrading or just the mix shifting?), then decide — retrain, recalibrate, or fix the pipeline — documenting each step for the model risk review.
Retrain immediately on the new data; investigation wastes time.
Do nothing; models are allowed to change their minds.
Blame the demographic segment and exclude it from scoring.
scenarios.why: Drift investigation is differential diagnosis: data drift, pipeline breakage, concept drift, or mix shift each imply a different fix, and retraining on a broken pipeline just bakes the breakage in. Monitor inputs first, outputs second, then act.
scenarios.hint: What changed: the world, the data feed, or the model?

scenarios.title: Latency versus quality
scenarios.situation: An LLM feature has two serving options: a large model at 8s P99 latency and $0.06/request with top quality, or a small model at 400ms P99 and $0.002/request with slightly lower quality. The feature is interactive chat; the budget allows $20k/month.
scenarios.prompt: How should the team decide?
choices: Decide from the product constraint: interactive chat needs sub-second response, and at scale the large model's cost/latency breaks both budget and UX — ship the small model (possibly with routing: small by default, large for flagged hard queries), and validate with A/B quality metrics that the 'slightly lower' quality is acceptable to users.
Always choose the largest model; quality is the only criterion and users will wait.
Always choose the cheapest; cost is the only criterion.
Run both on every request and average the answers.
scenarios.why: Serving is a three-way trade — quality, latency, cost — priced by the product's actual constraints. Interactive UX sets the latency budget, scale sets the cost budget, and quality is then maximized within both, often via routing rather than a single model.
scenarios.hint: What do the product's latency and cost budgets allow, before quality is even discussed?

scenarios.title: The notebook that became a service
scenarios.situation: A data scientist's notebook achieves 94% accuracy — then the 'deployment' is the notebook run by cron. No API, no monitoring, no versioning; the first schema change breaks it silently for a week.
evidence: Observed: A data scientist's notebook achieves 94% accuracy — then the 'deployment' is the notebook run by cron. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Close the prototype-production gap (2) Apply the production checklist Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What separates the notebook from the production system?
choices: A. Better notebooks; the tooling is the gap.

B. The production checklist: versioned data + code + model, an API contract (not a cron job), input validation, monitoring (quality + data + infra), rollback capability, and ownership — the notebook proves the idea; the system serves it reliably.
C. Higher accuracy; 94% was too low.
D. More cron jobs; scheduling is deployment.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the schema change broke it silently for a week. Which production practice would have screamed on day one?
scenarios.why: The notebook-to-production gap is the central theme of AI engineering: the notebook optimizes for experimentation (flexibility, visibility), production optimizes for reliability (contracts, monitoring, reversibility). The checklist converts one to the other: versioning (what data/code/model produced this behavior?), API contracts (typed inputs/outputs, not cell outputs), validation (reject the schema change loudly, not silently), monitoring (the eval-online lesson's quality tracking), rollback (the previous version deployable in minutes), and ownership (a human accountable for the system's behavior). Accuracy (choice C) was never the problem — 94% in a notebook is a demo; 94% behind an API with monitoring is a product.

scenarios.title: The model that never learns from users
scenarios.situation: The assistant serves 100K conversations a month — and learns nothing from them. The same failure modes repeat; the golden set is frozen at launch. The data flywheel is a data parking lot.
evidence: Observed: The assistant serves 100K conversations a month — and learns nothing from them. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Build data flywheels (2) Close the improvement loop Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What builds the flywheel?
choices: A. More launch data; the initial set was small.

B. The improvement loop: production signals (thumbs down, corrections, escalations) captured as training signal, human review of the valuable failures, curated additions to the golden set and training data, retraining/fine-tuning on the improved data, and redeploy with regression gates — the system compounds; each month's failures become next month's training.
C. Bigger models; the flywheel is model scale.
D. User data is too noisy; ignore it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 100K conversations a month, zero learning. Which loop stage is missing first?
scenarios.why: The flywheel is the compounding loop: production use generates the highest-value data (real failures, real edge cases, real user language) — but only if captured, reviewed, curated, and trained on. The loop's stages: signal capture (implicit: corrections, escalations, abandonment; explicit: ratings), human review (the valuable failures triaged — not all signal is gold), curation (failures become golden-set items and training examples — the eval loop closes AND the training loop opens), retraining (SFT/preference tuning on the curated data), and redeploy behind regression gates (the improvement must not break what worked). The frozen golden set (the scenario's symptom) is the loop's absence made visible.

scenarios.title: The audit nobody can answer
scenarios.situation: Regulators ask: 'What data trained this model? Which version is in production? Who approved the change?' The team answers with Slack threads and vibes — no inventory exists of data, models, prompts, or approvals.
evidence: Observed: Regulators ask: 'What data trained this model? Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Maintain AI BOMs (2) Answer audits with queries Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct AI system inventory?
choices: A. Good documentation culture; write more docs.

B. The AI Bill of Materials: a versioned inventory of every component (training data sources + versions, base model + adapters, prompts + versions, eval datasets + results, deployment config, approval records) — generated by the pipeline, not written by hand; the audit answer is a query, not an archaeology project.
C. The audit is unlikely; ignore it.
D. Open-source everything; transparency by default.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the answers must exist BEFORE the audit. What records them automatically?
scenarios.why: The audit questions are answerable only if the answers were recorded at build time — Slack archaeology after the fact is not a system. The AI BOM is the versioned inventory: every training data source (with version/hash), the base model and every adapter (with training configs), every prompt template (versioned), every eval dataset and its results per model version, the deployment configuration, and the approval records (who signed off on what, when). Generated by the pipeline (the training run writes its BOM entry; the deploy writes its) — hand-written docs (choice A) rot; generated inventories do not. The audit becomes a database query; the incident response ('which customers saw model v3?') becomes answerable.

scenarios.title: The 2 AM model incident
scenarios.situation: At 2 AM the assistant starts giving wrong refund amounts — a bad prompt deploy. Nobody knows the rollback command, the on-call cannot tell if it is the model or the data, and the incident channel debates while money leaks.
evidence: Observed: At 2 AM the assistant starts giving wrong refund amounts — a bad prompt deploy. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Respond to AI incidents (2) Write AI runbooks Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct AI incident response?
choices: A. Wake the ML team; they will figure it out.

B. AI-adapted incident practice: runbooks for model incidents (rollback command first, not last), the trace as the diagnostic (which stage changed?), severity tied to behavioral impact, the BOM for blast-radius assessment (who got the bad version?), and postmortems that fix the deploy process — the 2 AM confusion is a runbook gap, not a talent gap.
C. Roll back everything always; safety first.
D. Incidents are rare in AI; skip the process.
scenarios.hint: Hint: at 2 AM, what should the on-call read FIRST — and does it exist?
scenarios.why: The 2 AM chaos had three fixable causes: no runbook (the rollback command lived in someone's head), no diagnostic path (the on-call could not distinguish model vs data vs prompt — the tracing lesson's stage attribution, unused), and no blast-radius data (the BOM would say exactly which version served which users when). AI incident practice adapts the software discipline: runbooks with the rollback FIRST (the one command that stops the bleeding), traces as the diagnostic (read the trace, find the guilty stage), severity by behavioral impact (wrong money > wrong tone), and postmortems targeting the process (why did the bad prompt deploy without a canary? — the release lesson's gate failed). 'Wake the ML team' (choice A) is the absence of a system.

scenarios.title: The deflection rate that hit 90%
scenarios.situation: The support assistant's 'deflection rate' hits 90% — leadership celebrates. But CSAT is falling: the bot deflects by ending conversations quickly ('Is there anything else?'), not by resolving issues. The metric became the target; the target ate the product.
evidence: Observed: The support assistant's 'deflection rate' hits 90% — leadership celebrates. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Detect metric gaming (2) Pair metrics with outcomes Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct production-metric discipline?
choices: A. The 90% is real; CSAT lags and will recover.

B. Counter-metric pairing + outcome measurement: every optimization metric gets a paired health metric (deflection WITH resolution/CSAT), the true outcome measured independently (did the customer's problem get solved? sampled and judged), and metric changes validated against the outcome — when deflection rises and resolution falls, the metric is lying.
C. Remove the deflection metric; metrics cause gaming.
D. Set the deflection target to 95%; push harder.
scenarios.hint: Hint: deflection rose while CSAT fell. Which one measures the customer's actual outcome?
scenarios.why: Goodhart's law in production: the deflection metric rewards ended conversations, so the system learns to end conversations — resolution is unmeasured, so it is unoptimized. The discipline: pair every target metric with its counter-metric (deflection + resolution rate + CSAT — the trio must move together), measure the true outcome independently (sample conversations, judge 'was the problem solved?' — the rubric-judge lesson applied to business outcomes), and treat metric/outcome divergence as the highest-priority alert (the dashboard's most important panel is the gap between the metric and the outcome). Removing metrics (choice C) blinds the team; pushing the target (choice D) accelerates the gaming.

scenarios.title: The quality win users hated
scenarios.situation: The team upgrades to a larger model: quality scores rise 8%, but p95 latency triples to 9 seconds. Engagement drops — users preferred the faster, slightly dumber answers. The quality metric won; the product lost.
evidence: Observed: The team upgrades to a larger model: quality scores rise 8%, but p95 latency triples to 9 seconds. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Manage latency-quality trade-offs (2) Design tiered serving Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct latency-quality discipline?
choices: A. Quality is king; users will adapt to the latency.

B. Joint optimization with user-measured trade-offs: latency SLOs set from user tolerance (measured, not assumed), the quality-latency frontier mapped (each candidate model/optimization plotted), tiered serving (fast model default, strong model on demand), and A/B validation of the actual user impact — the 8% quality gain priced against the engagement loss.
C. The biggest model always; latency is an infra problem.
D. The smallest model always; speed is everything.
scenarios.hint: Hint: engagement dropped when latency tripled. What experiment prices the 8% quality gain against that?
scenarios.why: Quality and latency are not independent virtues — they trade off along a frontier, and the product lives at a point on it, not at either extreme. The discipline: measure user latency tolerance (the engagement drop at 9s is data — find the knee), map the frontier (each model size, quantization level, and optimization plotted as quality-vs-latency points), serve in tiers (the fast model answers by default; the strong model handles the hard/escalated cases — the deployment lesson's routing), and validate with users (A/B the trade-off — the 8% gain vs the engagement loss, measured, not debated). The infra-only view (choice C) ignores that some latency is model-inherent; the speed-only view (choice D) ignores that quality drives retention.

scenarios.title: The IL-12 AI Engineering Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that IL-12 AI Engineering is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in IL-12 AI Engineering?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — IL-12 AI Engineering issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — IL-12 AI Engineering is too complex to troubleshoot systematically

domains.name: LLM Fundamentals
domains.description: Tokens, transformers, context windows, and inference parameters — how large language models actually work.

scenarios.title: The bill that did not match the word count
scenarios.situation: An API bill shows 2M tokens for 500K words of English text. The team budgeted by words and is shocked — and their 'max 1000 words' truncation produces inconsistent cutoffs across languages.
objectives: Budget and truncate in token space
evidence: Observed: An API bill shows 2M tokens for 500K words of English text. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Count tokens accurately (2) Budget and truncate in token space Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct mental model?
choices: A. Tokens equal words; the vendor is overcharging.

B. Subword tokenization (BPE/WordPiece): common words are one token, rare words split into several; ratios vary by language (~1.3 tokens/word English, far higher for code/CJK). Budget, truncate, and set max_tokens in TOKENS — and count with the model's actual tokenizer (tiktoken), not word counts.
C. Truncate by characters; characters are universal.
D. Tokens are only a billing concept; they do not affect the model.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the model reads token IDs, not words. What unit does the bill use?
scenarios.why: LLMs never see words or characters — they see token IDs from a fixed vocabulary (~100K entries) built by byte-pair encoding: frequent strings (' the') are single tokens, rare ones split ('antidisestablishmentarianism' -> many). This makes the word-to-token ratio variable: ~0.75 words/token in English prose, far worse in code, other languages, or with lots of whitespace. Billing, context limits, and max_tokens all operate in tokens — budgeting in words guarantees surprises, and truncating '1000 words' cuts different amounts of meaning per language. The fix is mechanical: count with tiktoken (the actual tokenizer) before sending, and think in tokens everywhere the API does.

scenarios.title: The interviewer asks 'what is attention?'
scenarios.situation: In an AI engineering interview: 'Explain attention in one minute, and why the transformer replaced RNNs.' The candidate recites the formula without the intuition.
evidence: Observed: In an AI engineering interview: 'Explain attention in one minute, and why the transformer replaced RNNs.' The candidate recites the formula without the intuition. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain attention intuitively (2) Explain why transformers scaled Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct explanation?
choices: A. Attention is a weighted average; transformers are just bigger RNNs.

B. Attention lets each token directly weight every other token's relevance (queries/keys/values) — capturing long-range dependencies in constant path length, and crucially it parallelizes across the sequence, unlike RNNs' sequential steps. That parallelism is what made internet-scale training feasible.
C. Attention is a type of convolution over text.
D. Transformers replaced RNNs because they have more parameters.
scenarios.hint: Hint: what could RNNs not do that made training at internet scale impossible?
scenarios.why: The RNN's bottleneck was sequential: token 1000's representation depended on 999 prior steps, unparallelizable and with gradients decaying over distance. Attention removes the sequence: each position computes relevance scores against ALL positions (query-key dot products, softmaxed into weights) and takes a weighted sum of values — 'bank' attends to 'river' vs 'money' based on context, in one step. Multi-head attention runs several such relevance computations in parallel (different heads learn different relations: syntax, coreference, etc.). The parallelizability across the sequence is the economic breakthrough: transformers train on thousands of GPUs simultaneously; RNNs could not. Parameters (choice D) followed scale; parallelism enabled it.

scenarios.title: The 200K context that forgot the middle
scenarios.situation: The team stuffs 200K tokens of documents into a long-context model and asks a question about a paragraph in the middle. The answer is wrong or hallucinated — despite the context 'fitting.'
evidence: Observed: The team stuffs 200K tokens of documents into a long-context model and asks a question about a paragraph in the middle. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain lost-in-the-middle (2) Choose RAG vs long context Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct understanding of long context?
choices: A. The model reads all 200K tokens equally; the prompt must be wrong.

B. 'Lost in the middle': models attend best to the start and end of long contexts, worst to the middle — plus cost/latency scale with length. The fix: retrieve-then-read (RAG) to put the relevant chunk where the model looks, keep prompts focused, and test with needle-in-haystack evals before trusting long context.
C. Longer context is always better; add more documents.
D. Context windows are marketing; models ignore long inputs.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the paragraph was IN the context. Where in the context was it?
scenarios.why: Fitting is not attending: benchmark studies ('lost in the middle') show retrieval accuracy degrades significantly for information in the middle of long contexts — the model's attention is effectively U-shaped. More context also costs more (per-token pricing on the full input, every call) and answers slower (quadratic attention). The engineering response is selectivity: RAG retrieves the relevant few thousand tokens and presents them compactly (ideally near the start/end), instead of dumping the corpus and hoping. Long context is for when you cannot pre-select (whole-codebase reasoning, long conversations) — and then you verify with needle-in-haystack tests, not assumptions.

scenarios.title: The creative model that could not do math
scenarios.situation: The team uses temperature 1.2 for everything ('more creative'). Their invoice-extraction pipeline returns different totals on every run, and the eval scores swing wildly between runs.
evidence: Observed: The team uses temperature 1.2 for everything ('more creative'). Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Set sampling per task (2) Make evaluated pipelines deterministic Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct parameter discipline?
choices: A. Temperature 1.2 everywhere; creativity is always good.

B. Match sampling to the task: temperature ~0 (greedy) for extraction/classification/factual tasks (deterministic, reproducible); moderate temperature (0.7-1.0) for creative writing; top-p as the alternative nucleus control. Nondeterminism in extraction is a bug, not creativity.
C. Always temperature 0; sampling is never useful.
D. Parameters do not matter; the model decides.
scenarios.hint: Hint: should invoice totals vary between runs? What parameter made them vary?
scenarios.why: Temperature rescales the output distribution: near 0 collapses to the most likely token at each step (deterministic, reproducible — what extraction needs); higher values sample more broadly (diverse, creative — what brainstorming wants). The invoice pipeline at 1.2 samples different phrasings AND different numbers per run — the totals vary because the task got randomness it never asked for. Top-p (nucleus sampling) is the companion control: sample from the smallest set covering probability p, cutting the long tail of weird tokens. Always-0 (choice C) kills legitimate creative uses; the discipline is task-matched sampling, with temperature 0 as the default for anything evaluated or reproduced.

scenarios.title: The confident wrong citation
scenarios.situation: The support bot answers a refund question with a confident, detailed — and entirely fabricated — policy citation. The customer quotes it back; legal is unhappy.
evidence: Observed: The support bot answers a refund question with a confident, detailed — and entirely fabricated — policy citation. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.

Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Architect against hallucination (2) Verify claims against sources Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct anti-hallucination architecture?
choices: A. Tell the model 'do not hallucinate' in the system prompt; instruction suffices.

B. Grounding + verification: RAG over the actual policy docs (the model answers FROM retrieved text), require citations to retrieved chunks, add a verification pass (does the answer's claim appear in the sources?), and design the fallback ('I don't have that information') as a first-class response — confidence is not correctness.
C. Use a bigger model; scale eliminates hallucinations.
D. Hallucinations are unavoidable; ship and apologize.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the model answered confidently about a policy it never saw. What would have let it SEE the policy?
scenarios.why: Hallucination is the model's default mode: it generates plausible text, and plausibility is not truth — a bigger model (choice C) hallucinates more fluently, not less. 'Do not hallucinate' (choice A) is a wish, not a mechanism; instruction-following does not create knowledge the model lacks. The architecture is grounding: the answer must come FROM retrieved sources (RAG), with citations the user (and the verification pass) can check — a claim without a supporting chunk is rejected or flagged. The fallback ('I don't know') must be trained/allowed: models that are punished for uncertainty hallucinate instead; the system should reward abstention over fabrication.

scenarios.title: The 95% accuracy that was not
scenarios.situation: A vendor claims '95% accuracy on industry benchmarks.' Your eval on YOUR data shows 71%. The vendor's benchmark was a public dataset, possibly in the training data, measuring a different task distribution.
objectives: Evaluate vendors on your own data
evidence: Observed: A vendor claims '95% accuracy on industry benchmarks.' Your eval on YOUR data shows 71%. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Evaluate vendors on your own data Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response to benchmark claims?
choices: A. Trust the vendor; benchmarks are standardized.

B. Evaluate on YOUR data, YOUR task, YOUR distribution: build a golden dataset from real production inputs, measure the metric that matters to the business, and treat vendor benchmarks as marketing — contaminated (training-data overlap), distribution-mismatched, and metric-gamed.
C. The 71% must be your implementation's fault; the vendor is right.
D. Average the two numbers; the truth is in the middle.
scenarios.hint: Hint: whose data was the 95% measured on?
scenarios.why: Public benchmarks suffer three corruptions: contamination (the benchmark was in the training data — the model memorized it), distribution mismatch (the benchmark's task mix differs from yours), and metric gaming (optimizing for the benchmark's metric, not your business outcome). The only number that matters is performance on YOUR inputs for YOUR task — which requires YOUR golden dataset, built from production samples and labeled to your quality bar. Vendor benchmarks are useful for rough tiering (is this model class plausible?) and useless for procurement decisions. The 71% is the truth about your use case; the 95% is the truth about the vendor's marketing.

domains.name: Prompt Engineering
domains.description: System prompts, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured output, and prompt testing — the engineering discipline of instructing models.

scenarios.title: The support bot with no identity
scenarios.situation: The support bot sometimes claims to be human, sometimes refuses to answer product questions, and its tone swings wildly. There is no system prompt — each user message starts cold.
evidence: Observed: The support bot sometimes claims to be human, sometimes refuses to answer product questions, and its tone swings wildly. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Write effective system prompts (2) Test prompt rules Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What does a good system prompt do?
choices: A. Nothing important; the user prompt carries the task.

B. Define identity, scope, rules, and output contract up front: who the assistant is, what it may/must not do, the domain boundaries, tone, and the response format — the system prompt is the persistent instruction layer every turn inherits.
C. Make it as long as possible; detail equals quality.
D. System prompts are only for jailbreak protection.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the bot's behavior varied per conversation. What persists across turns that could fix it?
scenarios.why: The system prompt is the model's standing orders: identity ('You are Acme's support assistant'), scope ('answer product questions; refuse medical/legal advice'), rules ('never claim to be human; cite sources'), and format ('respond in the JSON schema'). Without it, each turn is a cold start — the model improvises identity and boundaries per conversation, producing the observed swings. Good system prompts are concise and load-bearing: every line earns its tokens (they are charged on EVERY call). Bloat (choice C) wastes budget and dilutes attention; the discipline is minimal-sufficient instruction.

scenarios.title: The classifier that ignored the instructions
scenarios.situation: A ticket classifier gets a long instruction describing 12 categories with rules. Accuracy is 62% — the model confuses similar categories despite the detailed spec.
evidence: Observed: A ticket classifier gets a long instruction describing 12 categories with rules. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Apply few-shot prompting (2) Target examples at confusions Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What improves it most?
choices: A. Longer instructions; the spec needs more detail.

B. Few-shot examples: 2-3 labeled examples PER confusing category, showing the input and the correct label (with brief reasoning) — examples teach the decision boundary that prose describes poorly; instructions tell, examples show.
C. More categories; granularity helps.
D. Higher temperature; the model needs creativity.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the model read the rules and still confused the categories. What teaches a boundary better than rules?
scenarios.why: Prose describes categories abstractly; examples demonstrate the boundary: the model sees 'this borderline ticket -> Category B (because X)' and generalizes the pattern far better than from rules alone. The confusing pairs are the target — add examples precisely where the errors cluster (the confusion matrix tells you where). 2-3 diverse examples per category beat 20 similar ones (diversity covers the boundary); and brief reasoning in the example ('-> B, because the issue is billing not technical') teaches the WHY, not just the label. Longer specs (choice A) hit diminishing returns fast — the model already read the rules; it needs to SEE them applied.

scenarios.title: The math word problem it got wrong
scenarios.situation: The model answers multi-step reasoning questions (pricing calculations, logic puzzles) incorrectly — jumping straight to an answer with no working shown. Accuracy on 3-step problems is 40%.
evidence: Observed: The model answers multi-step reasoning questions (pricing calculations, logic puzzles) incorrectly — jumping straight to an answer with no working shown. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Apply chain-of-thought (2) Weigh the cost/accuracy tradeoff Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What improves multi-step reasoning?
choices: A. Bigger model; reasoning is parametric.

B. Chain-of-thought: prompt the model to reason step by step BEFORE the final answer ('Let's work through this step by step'), optionally with a worked example — the intermediate tokens are working memory; accuracy on multi-step tasks jumps because each step is computed explicitly instead of in one leap.
C. Lower temperature; the leaps are sampling noise.
D. Shorter prompts; the model is distracted.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the model leapt to the answer. What would let it show its work — and why does showing work help?
scenarios.why: The model's computation per token is fixed — a direct answer forces all reasoning into one leap, while step-by-step tokens give it scratch space: each step's output becomes context for the next, exactly like human working memory. The phrase 'let's think step by step' (zero-shot CoT) or a worked example (few-shot CoT) elicits this reliably, often doubling accuracy on arithmetic/logic benchmarks. Temperature (choice C) is orthogonal — the issue is missing intermediate computation, not sampling noise. Cost note: CoT uses more output tokens (the reasoning is billed) — worth it where accuracy matters, wasteful where it does not.

scenarios.title: The parser that broke on prose
scenarios.situation: The pipeline asks the model for JSON, then json.loads() the response. It works until the model adds 'Here is the JSON:' preamble or a trailing explanation — the parser crashes, the pipeline halts, on 3% of calls.
evidence: Observed: The pipeline asks the model for JSON, then json.loads() the response. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Constrain output with schemas (2) Validate every response Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct structured-output discipline?
choices: A. Regex the JSON out of the prose; parsing prose is fine.

B. Constrain the output: JSON mode / response_format with a schema (or function-calling with defined parameters) — the model generates ONLY schema-valid JSON; validate against the schema on receipt and retry on failure. Prose never enters the pipeline.
C. Ask nicely for 'only JSON'; politeness works.
D. Parse with a lenient parser; crashes are the parser's fault.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the pipeline needs a CONTRACT, not a request. What enforces the contract at generation time?
scenarios.why: Free-text generation around JSON is nondeterministic formatting — 'Here is...' today, markdown fences tomorrow, an apology paragraph next week. Constrained decoding (JSON mode, response_format: json_schema, function calling) makes the schema a generation constraint: the output IS valid JSON matching the schema, by construction, not by hope. The pipeline then validates (pydantic/jsonschema) and retries the tiny failure remainder — the 3% becomes ~0%. Regex extraction (choice A) is the arms race you lose; politeness (choice C) is not a contract.

scenarios.title: The prompt tweak that broke production
scenarios.situation: Someone 'improves' the prompt wording on Friday; by Monday, extraction accuracy dropped 8 points. No test caught it — there were no prompt tests. The rollback is a git guess.
evidence: Observed: Someone 'improves' the prompt wording on Friday; by Monday, extraction accuracy dropped 8 points. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Version prompts (2) Gate prompt changes on evals Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct prompt-engineering discipline?
choices: A. Do not touch prompts in production; freeze them forever.

B. Prompts as versioned, tested artifacts: the prompt lives in git, a golden evaluation set runs on every change (accuracy/latency/cost vs the baseline), and regressions block the deploy — the prompt is code, with code's CI.
C. Test prompts manually by reading a few outputs; eyeballing suffices.
D. Prompts cannot be tested; accept the risk.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the tweak changed EVERY output. What catches a change to every output?
scenarios.why: Prompts are the most leveraged code in an LLM system — one wording change shifts every output — yet teams edit them like chat messages. The discipline treats them as code: versioned in git (diffs, blame, rollback), evaluated against a golden set (labeled examples covering the task's range, run automatically), with the deploy gated on no-regression (accuracy within tolerance, latency/cost bounded). The Friday tweak then fails CI on Monday-morning's terms — caught before deploy, not after. Eyeballing (choice C) samples 3 outputs out of thousands; the eval set samples the distribution.

scenarios.title: The demo prompt that died in production
scenarios.situation: The demo prompt is perfect on 10 hand-picked examples. In production, on real user inputs (typos, edge cases, adversarial), it fails 30% of the time — the dev examples never represented the distribution.
evidence: Observed: The demo prompt is perfect on 10 hand-picked examples. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Develop prompts against real distributions Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct prompt-development process?
choices: A. The demo was misleading; prompts do not work in production.

B. Develop against the real distribution: sample production inputs for the dev set, include adversarial/edge cases from day one, and measure on a held-out eval set — the 10 hand-picked examples are the demo, not the development set.
C. More hand-picked examples; 10 was too few.
D. Constrain user inputs to match the dev examples.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the 10 examples represented the developer, not the users. What represents the users?
scenarios.why: Hand-picked dev examples are a biased sample: clean, representative of the developer's imagination, blind to the production distribution's typos, edge cases, and adversaries. The process fix: sample REAL inputs (anonymized production logs) for development, deliberately include the ugly cases (the eval set's adversarial slice), and hold out a separate eval set the prompt never sees during iteration. The 30% failure rate was knowable on day one — with the right dev set. The demo is for stakeholders; the distribution-sampled set is for engineering.

domains.name: Data Pipelines for ML
domains.description: Ingestion, labeling, leakage prevention, versioning, and training-serving parity — the data discipline behind reliable models.

scenarios.title: The pipeline that worked on a laptop
scenarios.situation: The ingestion script reads CSVs with pandas on a laptop. On the full 2TB event firehose it OOMs, takes 3 days, and silently drops malformed rows — the training set is a biased sample of 'rows that parsed.'
evidence: Observed: The ingestion script reads CSVs with pandas on a laptop. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Design schema-enforced ingestion (2) Add quality gates Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct ingestion architecture?
choices: A. Bigger laptop; the script is fine.

B. Distributed, schema-enforced ingestion: stream/batch framework (Spark/Beam) processing in partitions, explicit schemas with a dead-letter queue for malformed rows (counted and alerted, not silently dropped), idempotent reruns, and data-quality checks (row counts, null rates, distributions) at every stage.
C. Sample the firehose; models do not need all the data.
D. Skip validation; speed matters more than correctness.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the training set was 'rows that parsed.' What did the model never see?
scenarios.why: Laptop-scale tooling (pandas, in-memory) collapses on production volumes — and the silent row-dropping is the worse failure: the model trains on a biased subset (well-formed rows), learning a distribution that does not match reality. The architecture: partitioned distributed processing (the data never fits one machine), schemas enforced at ingestion (malformed rows go to a dead-letter queue WITH counts and alerts — visible, not silent), idempotent stages (reruns are safe), and quality gates (expect row counts within bounds, null rates below thresholds, distribution drift flagged). Sampling (choice C) is legitimate for exploration, not as a substitute for processing the full training set.

scenarios.title: The model that predicted the past
scenarios.situation: A churn model scores 0.97 AUC in validation — and 0.61 in production. Investigation: features included 'days since last login' computed AT PREDICTION TIME in training (using future logins), but at serving time only past logins exist.
evidence: Observed: A churn model scores 0.97 AUC in validation — and 0.61 in production. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Prevent temporal leakage (2) Enforce point-in-time features Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what is the correct discipline?
choices: A. The model overfit; add regularization.

B. Temporal leakage: training features used information unavailable at serving time. The fix is point-in-time correctness — every feature computed as-of the prediction timestamp (feature stores with event timestamps, backfills respecting time), plus a serving-time feature audit.
C. The validation set was too easy; make it harder.
D. Leakage is unavoidable; discount all offline metrics by 30%.
scenarios.hint: Hint: in training, the feature 'knew' the future. At serving time, what does it know?
scenarios.why: Leakage is not overfitting — it is time travel: the training features contained the future ('days since last login' counted logins that happened AFTER the prediction moment), so the model learned to 'predict' churn using information that will not exist when it serves. Offline metrics then measure a fantasy, and production measures reality — the 0.97-to-0.61 cliff is the signature. The discipline is point-in-time correctness: every feature value must be computable from data available AT the prediction timestamp. Feature stores enforce this (event-sourced features with timestamps, backfills that respect the as-of time); the audit replays serving-time feature computation on historical data to prove parity.

scenarios.title: The 90% accurate labels
scenarios.situation: A classifier plateaus at 82% accuracy. Error analysis shows 15% of the TRAINING labels are wrong — the model learned the annotators' mistakes. More data will just teach more mistakes.
evidence: Observed: A classifier plateaus at 82% accuracy. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Measure label quality (2) Run the annotation quality loop Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct labeling discipline?
choices: A. More data; volume overcomes label noise.

B. Label quality as engineering: clear annotation guidelines with edge-case examples, annotator agreement measurement (inter-rater reliability), adjudication for disagreements, and golden test questions that catch drifting annotators — the model's ceiling is the labels' quality.
C. Use a bigger model; capacity overcomes bad labels.
D. Labels are subjective; accept the plateau.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the model learned the wrong answers. Where did the wrong answers come from?
scenarios.why: The model's ceiling is label quality: with 15% wrong labels, the 'correct' answer is wrong 15% of the time — the model cannot exceed the noise, and more data (choice A) teaches more mistakes faster. Labeling is a measurement process needing metrology: written guidelines (with the borderline examples that cause disagreement), multiple annotators per item with agreement scores (Cohen's kappa / raw agreement), adjudication workflows for conflicts, and golden questions (items with known answers seeded into the queue) that detect annotator drift or gaming. Clean a sample, measure the delta: the accuracy jump from relabeling usually dwarfs the jump from more data or bigger models.

scenarios.title: The model nobody can reproduce
scenarios.situation: The production model beats the challenger — but nobody can reproduce the training set: the SQL query changed, the raw files were overwritten, and the preprocessing script was edited in place. The 'winning' model is irreproducible.
evidence: Observed: The production model beats the challenger — but nobody can reproduce the training set: the SQL query changed, the raw files were overwritten, and the preprocessing script was edited in place. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Version datasets immutably (2) Write run manifests Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct data versioning practice?
choices: A. Save a copy of the final CSV; that is the version.

B. Version data like code: immutable dataset snapshots (content-addressed storage), versioned pipelines (git), and a manifest linking model -> dataset version -> code version -> params — reproducibility means re-running the exact inputs, not approximating them.
C. Versioning data is overkill; models are the asset.
D. Trust the experiment tracker; it logged the metrics.
scenarios.hint: Hint: to reproduce the training, what do you need besides the model code?
scenarios.why: An ML result without reproducible inputs is anecdote: the 'winning' model cannot be audited, debugged, or legally defended if its training data is unrecoverable. Data versioning mirrors code versioning: raw data immutable and content-addressed (DVC, lakeFS, or object-store versioning — overwrites create new versions, never mutate), pipelines in git (the SQL and preprocessing are code), and a manifest per training run binding model version to dataset version to code commit to hyperparameters. The final-CSV copy (choice A) loses the lineage (which raw? which pipeline version?) — reproducibility needs the chain, not just the endpoint.

scenarios.title: The feature that behaved differently live
scenarios.situation: Training computed 'average session length' over 30 days; serving computes it over the last 100 sessions (an optimization). The distributions differ subtly — the model degrades 5 points with no code change and no data drift.
evidence: Observed: Training computed 'average session length' over 30 days; serving computes it over the last 100 sessions (an optimization). Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Eliminate training-serving skew (2) Test feature parity Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct parity discipline?
choices: A. Retrain on the serving computation; the model will adapt.

B. Single feature logic, dual execution: the transformation defined ONCE (shared library / feature store) and executed in both training (batch) and serving (online) — skew is a code-duplication bug; the fix is one definition, two runtimes.
C. Skew is inevitable; monitor and retrain often.
D. Make serving match training by slowing serving down.
scenarios.hint: Hint: two implementations of one feature. How many should there be?
scenarios.why: Training-serving skew is the silent killer: the model learns P(outcome | training-features), but serving feeds it differently-computed features — the 5-point drop with 'no changes' is the signature. The root cause is duplicated logic: two implementations of 'average session length' that drifted (30 days vs 100 sessions). The fix is definitional unity: the feature logic lives ONCE (a shared library imported by both the batch pipeline and the serving code, or a feature store computing both), with parity tests asserting batch and online computations agree on sample inputs. Retraining on the skewed serving features (choice A) bakes the inconsistency in — the next 'optimization' breaks it again.

scenarios.title: The silent data outage
scenarios.situation: The upstream event producer changes its schema. The pipeline keeps running — parsing the new field as null, training on garbage for three weeks. No alert fired; the pipeline was 'green.'
evidence: Observed: The upstream event producer changes its schema. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Monitor data quality Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct pipeline monitoring?
choices: A. Green pipelines are fine; the model retraining will fix it.

B. Data observability: schema-change detection (alert on unexpected fields/types), volume/completeness monitors (row counts vs baseline), distribution drift detection (feature stats vs training baseline), and data-quality SLAs — the pipeline's greenness must mean 'data is good,' not just 'the job ran.'
C. More frequent retraining; fresh models absorb bad data.
D. Pin the upstream schema; producers must never change.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the pipeline was green for three weeks of garbage. What was it actually checking?
scenarios.why: Job-success monitoring ('the pipeline ran') is necessary and radically insufficient — the schema change kept the job green while poisoning the data for three weeks. Data observability monitors the DATA: schema expectations (new field? type change? -> alert), volume (row counts within baseline bands), completeness (null rates), and distribution (feature statistics vs the training baseline — drift detected statistically). The 'green' dashboard must be redefined: green means the data passed its quality contract, not that the cron fired. Retraining on garbage (choice C) just bakes the poison in faster.

domains.name: Vector Databases
domains.description: Embeddings, similarity search, indexing, and hybrid retrieval — the storage layer behind semantic search and RAG.

scenarios.title: The keyword search that missed everything
scenarios.situation: Support search matches keywords: 'refund' finds 'refund policy' but misses 'money back guarantee' and 'return process' — same meaning, different words. Customers cannot find answers that exist.
evidence: Observed: Support search matches keywords: 'refund' finds 'refund policy' but misses 'money back guarantee' and 'return process' — same meaning, different words. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Explain embeddings (2) Run semantic search Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What do embeddings change?
choices: A. Better keywords; the synonym list needs work.

B. Embeddings map text to dense vectors where semantic similarity = geometric proximity — 'refund' and 'money back' land near each other in vector space. Search becomes nearest-neighbor lookup by meaning, not string matching; the synonym list is replaced by geometry.
C. Embeddings are just compression; keywords still rule.
D. Translate everything to English first; then keywords work.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 'money back guarantee' shares no words with 'refund policy.' What representation makes them neighbors?
scenarios.why: Embedding models (trained on massive text) place semantically similar texts near each other in a high-dimensional space: cosine similarity between 'refund policy' and 'money back guarantee' vectors is high despite zero shared words. Search becomes: embed the query, find the k nearest document vectors — meaning-matched, language-agnostic (multilingual models), and robust to paraphrase. The synonym list (choice A) is the losing battle embeddings end: every paraphrase is already 'listed' by geometry. The tradeoff: embeddings need a vector index and are approximate (ANN), while keywords are exact — which is why production uses hybrid.

scenarios.title: The brute-force search that took 4 seconds
scenarios.situation: Semantic search over 10M vectors by exact comparison takes 4 seconds per query — unusable. The team considers fewer vectors ('just index the important docs').
evidence: Observed: Semantic search over 10M vectors by exact comparison takes 4 seconds per query — unusable. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Tune ANN indexes (2) Measure recall@k Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct indexing approach?
choices: A. Fewer vectors; 10M is too many to search.

B. Approximate nearest neighbor indexing (HNSW): a navigable graph index that finds near-neighbors in milliseconds by trading a tunable amount of recall — with parameters (M, efConstruction, efSearch) controlling the speed/recall frontier. 10M vectors in ~50ms is routine.
C. Exact search on GPUs; hardware solves it.
D. Shrink the vectors to 64 dims; smaller is faster.
scenarios.hint: Hint: 10M distance computations per query is the complexity. What changes the complexity class?
scenarios.why: Exact nearest-neighbor over 10M x 768-dim vectors is 10M distance computations per query — seconds, inevitably. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph: greedy traversal from the top layer descends to the query's neighborhood in logarithmic hops, examining a tiny fraction of vectors. The 'approximate' is tunable: efSearch (how many candidates to consider) trades latency for recall — measure recall@k on YOUR queries and set efSearch where the curve flattens. Fewer vectors (choice A) deletes the knowledge to dodge the engineering; GPUs (choice C) speed the brute force but do not fix the complexity class.

scenarios.title: The semantic search that missed the part number
scenarios.situation: Vector search finds conceptually related docs but misses exact part numbers ('XJ-4471'): the embedding treats it as generic alphanumeric noise. Technicians search by part number daily.
evidence: Observed: Vector search finds conceptually related docs but misses exact part numbers ('XJ-4471'): the embedding treats it as generic alphanumeric noise. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Build hybrid retrieval (2) Fuse with RRF Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct retrieval design?
choices: A. Vectors only; technicians should search conceptually.

B. Hybrid: vector search (semantic) + keyword/BM25 search (exact terms, part numbers, names) fused with reciprocal rank fusion — each covers the other's blind spot; the part number hits BM25, the concept hits vectors, fusion ranks both.
C. Keywords only; vectors are hype.
D. Two separate search boxes; let the user choose.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the query 'XJ-4471' is an exact token. The query 'how do I return this' is a concept. How many search paradigms do you need?
scenarios.why: Vectors and keywords fail differently: embeddings blur rare exact tokens (part numbers, error codes, names) into noise, while BM25 cannot match paraphrases. Production retrieval runs both and fuses: reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) combines the rankings without score normalization headaches — a document top-ranked by either signal surfaces. The part number query hits BM25 at rank 1; the conceptual query hits vectors at rank 1; RRF serves both from one box. Separate boxes (choice D) push the retrieval engineering onto the user — the product's job is one box that handles both.

scenarios.title: The retrieved doc the user cannot see
scenarios.situation: RAG retrieves a confidential HR document for a non-HR user — the vector search has no notion of permissions. The answer cites a document the user must never see.
evidence: Observed: RAG retrieves a confidential HR document for a non-HR user — the vector search has no notion of permissions. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Implement pre-filtering (2) Model access metadata Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct access-aware retrieval?
choices: A. Filter the answer text afterward; the retrieval can see everything.

B. Pre-filter by metadata: every chunk carries access metadata (departments, clearance, tenant); the vector query applies the filter BEFORE ranking (not after) — the user only ever retrieves what they may see. Post-filtering leaks via ranking and citations.
C. Separate vector DB per user; isolation by duplication.
D. Trust the model not to reveal it; the prompt says so.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the forbidden doc was RANKED before being hidden. When should it have been excluded?
scenarios.why: Post-filtering (retrieve-then-hide) is broken three ways: the hidden doc consumed a top-k slot (pushing visible docs out), its citation can leak in the answer, and the ranking was computed over forbidden content. Pre-filtering applies the access predicate inside the vector query (metadata filters are native to every vector DB): the search space itself excludes forbidden chunks, so rankings, citations, and answers are all clean by construction. Per-user DBs (choice C) explode operationally (10K users = 10K indexes); prompt-trust (choice D) is not a security boundary. The metadata (tenant_id, allowed_groups) must be assigned at ingestion — access control is a data-modeling decision, not a query hack.

scenarios.title: The chunk that answered half the question
scenarios.situation: Documents are chunked into fixed 500-token windows. A procedure split across a boundary retrieves only half the steps — the answer is confidently incomplete. Overlapping windows did not help; the split is in the wrong place.
evidence: Observed: Documents are chunked into fixed 500-token windows. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Chunk structure-aware (2) Evaluate chunking by recall Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct chunking strategy?
choices: A. Bigger fixed windows; 2000 tokens will cover it.

B. Structure-aware chunking: split on document structure (sections, headings, semantic boundaries) with small overlaps, keep procedures/lists intact, and attach section context (headers) to each chunk — the chunk is a coherent answer unit, not an arbitrary window.
C. One chunk per document; the model will find it.
D. Chunking does not matter; the model handles fragments.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the procedure was split across chunks. What in the document marks where procedures begin and end?
scenarios.why: Fixed windows split mid-thought: the procedure's steps 1-3 land in chunk A, 4-6 in chunk B, and neither chunk answers 'how do I do X' completely. Bigger windows (choice A) just move the boundary; the split-in-the-wrong-place problem is structural, not sized. Structure-aware chunking respects the document's own organization: sections/headings as natural boundaries, lists and procedures kept whole, each chunk prefixed with its section path ('Returns > International > Procedure') so the embedding carries context. Small overlaps (a sentence or two) catch the boundary cases; the goal is chunks that are independently answerable.

scenarios.title: The answer from last quarter's docs
scenarios.situation: The product docs update weekly; the vector index rebuilds monthly. RAG answers cite deprecated procedures — correct last quarter, wrong now. Users follow stale instructions.
evidence: Observed: The product docs update weekly; the vector index rebuilds monthly. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Keep indexes fresh Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct index-freshness discipline?
choices: A. Rebuild monthly; staleness is acceptable.

B. Incremental indexing tied to the source: document updates trigger re-embedding of changed chunks (CDC/webhooks), with version metadata per chunk and a freshness SLA — the index is a derived view of the source, kept in sync like any replica.
C. Delete old chunks manually when someone complains.
D. The model knows what is current; trust it.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the docs changed weekly, the index monthly. What syncs a replica to its source?
scenarios.why: A vector index is a derived replica of the source documents — and replicas need sync: change-data-capture (or CMS webhooks) on the source triggers re-chunking and re-embedding of exactly the changed documents, keeping the index fresh within the SLA (hours, not months). Version metadata per chunk (source version, indexed_at) makes staleness visible and debuggable; the freshness SLA ('index lags source by < 4h') is monitored like any other. Monthly rebuilds (choice A) guarantee a month of stale answers; manual deletion (choice C) scales to exactly one complaint.

domains.name: RAG Systems
domains.description: Retrieval-augmented generation done right: chunking, reranking, citations, evaluation, and knowing RAG's limits.

scenarios.title: The RAG demo that is not a product
scenarios.situation: The demo RAG answers questions over 50 PDFs beautifully. In production over 2M documents with permissions, updates, and latency SLAs, it retrieves junk, leaks access, cites stale docs, and takes 9 seconds.
evidence: Observed: The demo RAG answers questions over 50 PDFs beautifully. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Architect production RAG (2) Budget latency per stage Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What separates demo RAG from production RAG?
choices: A. A bigger vector DB; scale is the only gap.

B. The production concerns, each engineered: hybrid retrieval tuned on your queries, access pre-filtering, incremental indexing with freshness SLAs, reranking for precision, citation verification, latency budgets per stage, and evals gating every change — the demo proved the idea; the pipeline proves the product.
C. A bigger LLM; the retriever is fine.
D. More documents; coverage is the gap.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the demo had 50 docs and one user. List what production added — then what each addition demands.
scenarios.why: Demo RAG (50 PDFs, one user, no latency bound) exercises ~10% of the system: the production gaps are retrieval quality at scale (hybrid + reranking, tuned), access control (pre-filtering), freshness (incremental indexing), faithfulness (citation verification), latency (per-stage budgets: retrieve <200ms, rerank <300ms, generate bounded), and change safety (evals). Each gap is an engineered subsystem, not a tweak — the 9 seconds decompose into measurable stages, each with a budget and an owner. Bigger models (choice C) improve the generator while the retriever feeds it junk; the pipeline's quality is the retriever's quality.

scenarios.title: The top result that was irrelevant
scenarios.situation: Bi-encoder retrieval returns 50 candidates in 80ms, but the top 3 are often irrelevant — the bi-encoder is fast and coarse. The generator then writes confident answers from bad context.
evidence: Observed: Bi-encoder retrieval returns 50 candidates in 80ms, but the top 3 are often irrelevant — the bi-encoder is fast and coarse. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Build retrieve-rerank cascades (2) Measure ranking quality Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct two-stage retrieval?
choices: A. Bigger bi-encoder; the retriever needs capacity.

B. Retrieve-then-rerank cascade: fast bi-encoder for recall (50 candidates), precise cross-encoder reranker over the candidates (joint query-document encoding, far more accurate), top-k to the generator — speed from stage 1, precision from stage 2.
C. Skip retrieval; the generator is smart enough.
D. Return all 50 to the generator; more context is better.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the bi-encoder never lets the query and document MEET. What model does?
scenarios.why: Bi-encoders (separate query/doc vectors, dot product) are fast because the document vectors are precomputed — but the query and document never interact, so precision is coarse. Cross-encoders (query+document encoded JOINTLY through the transformer) model the interaction deeply — far more accurate, but too slow to run over millions of docs. The cascade gets both: bi-encoder narrows millions to 50 (recall), cross-encoder reranks 50 to 8 (precision), the generator sees only the best. All-50-to-generator (choice D) wastes the context window on 42 distractors — and distractors actively degrade generation (the lost-in-the-middle lesson).

scenarios.title: The answer that cited nothing
scenarios.situation: The RAG answer is correct-looking but cites no sources. When challenged, it cannot point to supporting text — and once, the 'correct' answer contradicted the retrieved docs (the model used its parametric memory instead).
evidence: Observed: The RAG answer is correct-looking but cites no sources. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Enforce faithful generation (2) Verify citations Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What enforces faithful generation?
choices: A. Trust the model; RAG implies grounding.

B. Citation requirements + verification: the prompt demands [n] citations to provided chunks, the pipeline verifies each cited chunk supports the claim (NLI/entailment check or a second model), and unsupported claims trigger regeneration or the fallback — the answer is checkable, not just plausible.
C. Longer retrieved context; more text means more faithful.
D. Citations are cosmetic; skip them.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the answer contradicted the retrieved docs. What check would have caught that before the user saw it?
scenarios.why: RAG without citation enforcement is ungrounded generation with extra steps: the model may ignore the chunks (parametric memory override) or blend them with hallucination, and the user cannot tell. The enforcement has two layers: generation-time (the prompt requires citations to specific chunks — 'cite [3] for this claim') and verification-time (each claim checked against its cited chunk via entailment — does chunk 3 actually support it?). Failures regenerate or fall back to 'I don't have that information.' More context (choice C) without enforcement just gives the model more to ignore; the verification pass is what makes citations load-bearing.

scenarios.title: The RAG improvement that was not
scenarios.situation: The team switches chunking strategies; the demo 'looks better.' Production metrics do not move. Three months later, a proper eval shows the change HURT recall 12% — the demo impressions were noise.
evidence: Observed: The team switches chunking strategies; the demo 'looks better.' Production metrics do not move. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Evaluate RAG properly (2) Gate changes on evals Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct RAG evaluation?
choices: A. Demo impressions; the team knows quality when they see it.

B. Golden QA set + retrieval and faithfulness metrics: curated question-answer-evidence triples from production queries, measuring context recall (is the answer IN the retrieved chunks?), faithfulness (does the answer follow the chunks?), and answer relevance — run on every pipeline change, gated like CI.
C. LLM-as-judge on 5 examples; quick and modern.
D. User thumbs-up only; the users decide.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the change hurt recall 12% for three months. What would have caught it on day one?
scenarios.why: Demo impressions sample 5 queries through human bias — the chunking change 'looked better' on the demo set while hurting the distribution. The eval set (hundreds of production-sampled questions with known-good answers AND the evidence chunks that support them) measures what matters: context recall (did retrieval find the supporting chunks?), faithfulness (did generation stay within them?), answer relevance. Frameworks (RAGAS, truLens, or hand-rolled) automate the scoring; the CI gate makes every pipeline change prove itself. Thumbs-up (choice D) is a lagging, sparse signal — useful, but not a change gate.

scenarios.title: The question RAG cannot answer
scenarios.situation: Users ask 'summarize Q3 revenue trends' — the answer needs aggregation over 10,000 rows, not passages. RAG retrieves 8 chunks about revenue and the model guesses the trend from fragments. Finance is furious.
evidence: Observed: Users ask 'summarize Q3 revenue trends' — the answer needs aggregation over 10,000 rows, not passages. Treat the situation above as the primary source — the correct decision must follow from these facts, not from generic best practice.
Success criteria for this scenario: (1) Know RAG's limits (2) Route questions by type Judge each option against these outcomes; the right answer is the one that satisfies all of them.
scenarios.prompt: What are RAG's boundaries, and what handles the rest?
choices: A. Bigger k; retrieve 800 chunks and the model will aggregate.

B. Route by question type: RAG for 'find and synthesize passages'; structured queries (SQL/text-to-SQL, pandas) for aggregation over rows; the router classifies the question and dispatches — retrieval over text cannot do arithmetic over 10K rows, and pretending it can produces confident fabrications.
C. Fine-tune the model on the revenue data; it will memorize the trends.
D. Tell users not to ask aggregation questions.
scenarios.hint: Hint: the question needed ARITHMETIC over rows. What tool does arithmetic over rows?
scenarios.why: RAG's contract is passage retrieval + synthesis: it answers 'what does the doc say about X' brilliantly and 'sum revenue by quarter' terribly — 8 chunks cannot represent 10,000 rows, and the model will happily extrapolate a trend from fragments (the confident fabrication finance caught). The architecture routes: a classifier (or the LLM itself, cheaply) decides passage-question vs data-question; data questions go to text-to-SQL / structured query paths that compute exactly; passage questions go to RAG. Fine-tuning (choice C) memorizes stale snapshots — the numbers change monthly; the query path computes live. 800 chunks (choice A) is the lost-in-the-middle problem at maximum cost.

scenarios.title: The $40K monthly RAG bill
