#        days_since_login = (as_of - last_login_before(as_of)).days
# The feature function takes the as-of time explicitly. Always.
example.walkthrough: The as-of parameter is the discipline made concrete: the feature function cannot see the future because it is only given the past up to the timestamp. 'today' (or now()) inside a feature function is the code smell — it silently advances with the calendar, leaking more with every backfill. Review every feature for hidden now() calls; that is the leakage audit.

pitfalls: now()/today inside feature code — the time machine; features must take explicit as-of timestamps.
Validating on leaked features — the 0.97 AUC fantasy; offline metrics on leaked data measure nothing.
'Discount offline metrics' fatalism — leakage is preventable with point-in-time discipline, not a tax to accept.
Ad-hoc backfill scripts — each script reimplements time-travel rules differently; the feature store centralizes the invariant.
lessons.try_it: Audit one feature pipeline for now() calls and future-information; rewrite the worst offender with an explicit as-of parameter.

lessons.title: Labeling and Annotation Quality
concepts: Annotation guidelines: written, with edge-case examples — the borderline cases cause the disagreements; specify them.
Inter-rater agreement: multiple annotators, measured agreement — low agreement names the ambiguous classes (fix the guidelines) or the weak annotators.
Adjudication: disagreements go to an expert tiebreak — the label is decided, not averaged.
Golden questions: known-answer items seeded in the queue — detect drift, gaming, and fatigue automatically.

example.code:
# Label quality loop:
# 1. guidelines v1 + 100 items x 3 annotators
# 2. agreement = 0.71 -> find the disagreeing classes
# 3. guidelines v2 (clarify those classes) + adjudicate conflicts
# 4. agreement = 0.89; golden questions live in the queue
# 5. Retrain: accuracy 82% -> 91%. The data was the model.
example.walkthrough: The loop is the method: measure agreement, find the disagreement source (ambiguous guidelines vs weak annotators), fix the source, adjudicate, and only then retrain. The 9-point jump came from zero new data and zero new parameters — pure label quality. This is the highest-ROI activity in most ML projects, and the least glamorous.

pitfalls: More data on bad labels — teaches mistakes at scale; quality before quantity.
Single annotator, no agreement measurement — the noise is invisible until error analysis finds it months later.
No adjudication — disagreements persist as noise; someone must decide.
Guidelines without edge cases — the easy cases never disagreed; the borderline examples are the specification.
lessons.try_it: Take 50 labeled items, relabel 10 yourself, and compute agreement — the gap is your label-noise estimate.

lessons.title: Data Versioning: Reproducible Datasets
concepts: Immutable raw data: versioned object storage / DVC / lakeFS — overwrites create versions; history is never mutated.
Pipelines in git: the SQL, the preprocessing, the feature code — versioned exactly like application code.
Run manifests: model v -> dataset v -> code commit -> params -> metrics — the complete reproducibility record per experiment.
The experiment tracker logs the manifest, not just metrics — metrics without inputs are unrepeatable.

example.code:
# The reproducibility contract (per training run):
# model: churn-v12
# dataset: s3://ml-data/churn/v7 (immutable, content hash: sha256:abc...)
# pipeline: git@a1b2c3d (sql/churn_features.sql, preprocess.py)
# params: configs/churn-v12.yaml
# Anyone with these four reproduces the run. Bit-for-bit.
example.walkthrough: The manifest is the contract: four pointers that fully determine the training. Content hashes (not 'latest') for data, git SHAs (not 'main') for code — every reference is pinned. This is also the compliance artifact: when asked 'what data trained this model?', the manifest answers precisely.

pitfalls: 'final.csv' as versioning — no lineage; the raw sources and pipeline versions are lost.
Mutable raw data — overwritten files destroy history; immutability is the rule.
Metrics without manifests — the tracker shows 0.91 AUC for a run nobody can repeat; log the inputs.
Unversioned pipeline edits — the SQL changed and nobody knows when; pipelines are code, in git.
lessons.try_it: Write the four-line manifest for your last (real or hypothetical) training run — the gaps are the findings.

lessons.title: Training-Serving Skew
concepts: One definition, two runtimes: feature logic written once, executed in batch (training) and online (serving) — duplication is the skew vector.
Parity tests: batch vs online computation asserted equal on fixtures — the test that catches the 30-days-vs-100-sessions drift.
Feature stores as the mechanism: the store computes and serves the same features; the application requests, not reimplements.
Skew monitoring in production: distribution comparison (training vs serving feature stats) — the alarm for the skew that slips through.

example.code:
# One definition:
# features/session.py: def avg_session_length(sessions, window_days=30)
# training: from features.session import avg_session_length  # batch
# serving:  from features.session import avg_session_length  # online
# test_parity: assert batch_fn(sample) == online_fn(sample)
example.walkthrough: The shared module is the single source of truth; both runtimes import it; the parity test pins their agreement on fixtures. The 'optimization' (100 sessions) now requires changing the shared definition — visible, tested, and applied to both runtimes simultaneously. Skew becomes a deliberate, reviewed change instead of a silent drift.

pitfalls: Duplicated feature logic — the 30-vs-100 drift; one definition or eventual skew.
Retraining onto skewed features — adapts to the inconsistency instead of fixing it; the next drift breaks it again.
'No changes' complacency — the 5-point drop with no code change IS the skew signal; investigate, do not retrain blindly.
No parity tests — the drift was undetectable until production metrics moved; fixtures catch it in CI.
lessons.try_it: Pick one feature computed in two places; unify the definition and write the parity test.

lessons.title: Embeddings: Meaning as Geometry
concepts: Embeddings = dense vectors (e.g. 768-3072 dims) where distance encodes semantic similarity — meaning as geometry.
Cosine similarity is the standard metric: angle between vectors, robust to magnitude — the nearest-neighbor query.
Embedding model choice matters: general vs domain-tuned, dimensionality vs cost, multilingual needs — the embedding IS the search quality.
Chunk before embedding: embed coherent passages (not whole documents) — the vector represents its chunk's meaning; oversized chunks blur it.

example.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
vecs = model.encode(["refund policy", "money back guarantee", "office lunch menu"])
# cosine(refund, money-back) >> cosine(refund, lunch): geometry knows.
example.walkthrough: The three vectors demonstrate the geometry: the two refund paraphrases are near each other, the lunch menu far — with no shared keywords. The query path is identical: embed the user's question, nearest-neighbor against the document vectors. Model choice (MiniLM vs larger) trades quality for speed/cost — benchmark on YOUR queries, not the model card's.

pitfalls: Keyword-only search for semantic needs — the synonym treadmill; paraphrases are infinite, geometry is not.
Embedding whole documents — the vector averages away the specific passage; chunk coherently first.
Ignoring the embedding model's domain fit — a general model on medical/legal text underperforms a tuned one; evaluate on your queries.
Exact-match expectations from ANN — approximate nearest neighbor trades perfect recall for speed; measure recall@k, not assumptions.
lessons.try_it: Embed 20 support articles + 5 paraphrased queries; check whether the right article is the nearest neighbor for each.

lessons.title: ANN Indexing: HNSW and the Speed/Recall Tradeoff
concepts: ANN (HNSW/IVF) replaces O(n) scan with graph/navigational search — milliseconds at 10M+ scale, with tunable recall.
HNSW parameters: M (graph degree), efConstruction (index-time thoroughness), efSearch (query-time recall/latency knob) — tune on YOUR recall@k.
Recall@k is the metric: fraction of true top-k found — measure it; 'approximate' is quantified, not hoped.
Index vs query tradeoff: bigger efConstruction = better graph = faster queries; pay at index time for query-time speed.

example.code:
# The tuning loop (conceptual):
# for efSearch in [16, 32, 64, 128, 256]:
#     recall = measure_recall_at_k(index, queries, efSearch)
#     latency = measure_p99(queries, efSearch)
# Pick the knee: recall >= 0.97 at minimal latency.
# Production: efSearch=64 -> 45ms p99, recall@10 = 0.98
example.walkthrough: The loop makes the tradeoff explicit and measured: each efSearch value gets a (recall, latency) point, and the knee of the curve is the operating point. The numbers are illustrative — YOUR curve on YOUR data decides. This is the discipline: 'approximate' with a measured recall number beats 'exact' that never ships.

pitfalls: Brute force at scale — the 4-second query; ANN is not optional past ~100K vectors.
Untuned efSearch — default parameters leave recall or latency on the table; the tuning loop is the job.
No recall measurement — 'it feels relevant' is not recall@k; the approximate needs its number.
Deleting vectors to dodge indexing — the knowledge loss is permanent; the index is the engineering answer.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark exact vs HNSW recall@10 and p99 latency on a 100K-vector sample; plot the efSearch curve.

lessons.title: Hybrid Search: Vectors + Keywords
concepts: BM25/keyword: exact terms, part numbers, codes, names — precise where vectors blur.
Vector: paraphrase, concept, cross-lingual — semantic where keywords are blind.
Reciprocal rank fusion: 1/(k+rank) summed across systems — fuses without normalizing incompatible scores.
Query analysis routes emphasis: detect exact-token queries (part numbers) vs conceptual ones — or just always run both; fusion is cheap.

example.code:
# Hybrid retrieval (pattern):
vec_hits = vector_search(query, k=50)      # semantic candidates
kw_hits  = bm25_search(query, k=50)        # exact-term candidates
fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion([vec_hits, kw_hits], k=60)
# 'XJ-4471' -> BM25 rank 1 -> fused top. 'return process' -> vector rank 1.
example.walkthrough: Both systems retrieve 50 candidates (cheap), RRF fuses the rankings — the part-number doc (BM25 #1) and the conceptual doc (vector #1) both surface at the top of the fused list. The k=60 constant in RRF dampens low ranks; tune it on your query set. This is the standard production pattern because the blind spots are complementary — together they cover the query space.

pitfalls: Vectors-only for exact-token queries — part numbers dissolve into embedding noise; the technicians' daily query fails.
Keywords-only for conceptual queries — the paraphrase problem from the embeddings lesson, unsolved.
Score averaging instead of rank fusion — vector and BM25 scores are incommensurable; RRF fuses ranks, not scores.
User-facing mode switches — 'semantic vs keyword' tabs; the product should fuse, not delegate.
lessons.try_it: Build the hybrid: run both retrievers on 20 queries (10 exact-token, 10 conceptual); compare each alone vs fused.

lessons.title: Metadata Filtering: Search Within Constraints
concepts: Pre-filter (metadata predicate in the query): the forbidden chunks never enter the candidate set — clean by construction.
Access metadata at ingestion: tenant, groups, clearance per chunk — assigned when the document is indexed, not at query time.
Post-filtering leaks: ranking pollution, citation leaks, wasted slots — filter before ranking, never after.
Tenant isolation for SaaS: tenant_id as a mandatory filter (or separate namespaces) — the cross-tenant leak is the catastrophic case.

example.walkthrough: The filter is part of the query, evaluated by the index before ranking: the HR document is excluded at the storage layer, so it cannot be ranked, cited, or leaked. The tenant filter is mandatory (never optional, never client-supplied) — the server injects the user's identity into every query. This is the pattern that makes RAG safe for multi-tenant, permissioned corpora.

pitfalls: Post-retrieval filtering — ranking pollution and citation leaks; the forbidden doc shaped the answer before being hidden.
Client-supplied filters — the user crafts their own tenant/groups; filters must be server-injected from auth.
Missing metadata at ingestion — retrofitting access labels onto 10M unlabeled chunks; model it on day one.
Prompt-based access control ('don't reveal HR docs') — not a security boundary; the model will cite what it retrieved.
lessons.try_it: Add access metadata to a chunk set; demonstrate that a forbidden query returns clean results with pre-filtering vs leaks with post-filtering.

lessons.title: Chunking Strategies for Retrieval
concepts: Structure-aware splitting: headings, sections, lists as boundaries — chunks align with the document's own organization.
Coherent answer units: each chunk should independently answer a plausible question — the retrievability test.
Context prefixes: section paths/headings prepended — the chunk's embedding carries its location in the document.
Small overlaps for boundary safety; evaluated, not assumed — chunking strategy is measured by retrieval recall, not aesthetics.

example.code:
# Structure-aware chunking (pattern):
# for section in parse_markdown(doc):           # headings = boundaries
#     for para in section.paragraphs:
#         chunk = f"[{doc.title} > {section.heading}]\n{para.text}"
#         # keep lists/procedures whole: never split inside a list
# evaluate: retrieval recall@k per strategy (fixed vs structural)
example.walkthrough: The parser (markdown/HTML-aware) yields the document's real structure; each chunk gets its section path as context; lists stay whole. The evaluation line is the discipline: chunking strategies are compared by retrieval recall on real questions, not by how tidy the code looks. Fixed windows are the baseline to beat — structure-aware usually wins by large margins on procedural content.

pitfalls: Fixed arbitrary windows — mid-procedure splits; the confidently-incomplete answer.
Bigger windows as the fix — moves the boundary, keeps the structural blindness.
No chunk evaluation — chunking chosen by aesthetics; measure recall@k per strategy.
Chunks without context — 'step 4: tighten it' embeds meaninglessly; the section path makes it retrievable.
lessons.try_it: Chunk one real document three ways (fixed, overlapping, structural); measure which retrieves best for 10 questions.

lessons.title: RAG Architecture: The Full Pipeline
concepts: Production RAG = demo RAG + retrieval quality (hybrid, rerank, tuned) + access control + freshness + faithfulness + latency budgets + evals.
Per-stage latency budgets: retrieve, rerank, generate each get a number — the 9 seconds become an itemized, attackable bill.
The retriever bounds quality: the generator cannot fix bad retrieval — invest in retrieval first, generation second.
Evals gate changes: every pipeline change (chunking, model, prompts) runs the golden set — RAG without evals rots silently.

example.code:
# Production RAG pipeline (stages + budgets):
# 1. query rewrite/expand          <50ms
# 2. hybrid retrieval (prefiltered) <200ms  -> 50 candidates
# 3. rerank (cross-encoder)         <300ms  -> top 8
# 4. generate (grounded, cited)     <2000ms
# 5. verify citations               <100ms
# Total budget: <3s. Each stage measured, each change eval-gated.
example.walkthrough: The stage list is the architecture and the latency budget in one: each stage has a number, so the 9-second problem becomes five optimizable problems. Reranking (cross-encoder over 50 candidates) is the precision step that demo RAG skips — bi-encoder retrieval is fast and coarse, the cross-encoder is slow and precise, and the cascade gets both. Citation verification closes the faithfulness loop from the hallucinations lesson.

pitfalls: Scaling the demo ('more docs, bigger DB') — the gaps are qualitative (access, freshness, evals), not just quantitative.
Generator-first investment — the retriever feeds the generator; bad retrieval caps the whole system.
No per-stage budgets — '9 seconds' as a monolith; itemize to optimize.
Change without evals — the chunking tweak that silently dropped recall 10 points; gate every change.
lessons.try_it: Instrument a RAG pipeline per stage; find which stage owns the latency and which owns the quality gap.

lessons.title: Reranking: Precision After Recall
concepts: Two-stage cascade: bi-encoder (fast, recall) -> cross-encoder (precise, rerank) — the standard production pattern.
Cross-encoders jointly encode query+document: the interaction modeling that bi-encoders cannot do — precision at the cost of speed.
Candidate count is the knob: 50-200 candidates balance rerank cost vs recall ceiling — tune on your nDCG.
nDCG@k measures ranking quality (not just recall): the reranker's metric — order matters, not just inclusion.

example.code:
# Rerank cascade:
# candidates = bi_encoder.retrieve(query, k=100)   # 80ms, coarse
# scored = cross_encoder.score([(query, c) for c in candidates])
# top8 = top_k(scored, 8)                        # +250ms, precise
# prompt = build(query, top8)                    # generator sees the best
example.walkthrough: The 100 candidates arrive fast and coarse; the cross-encoder scores each pair jointly (330ms for the batch on GPU); the top 8 are genuinely the most relevant. nDCG@8 on your eval set quantifies the win — typically a large jump over bi-encoder-only top-8. The cost (250ms) is why the cascade exists: cross-encoding 10M docs would take hours; over 100 candidates it takes a blink.

pitfalls: Bi-encoder-only top-k to the generator — coarse precision feeds the generator distractors; the confident-wrong answers.
Cross-encoder over the full corpus — accurate and impossibly slow; the cascade is the point.
All candidates to the generator — context dilution and lost-in-the-middle; the top-k exists to focus.
No ranking metric — 'feels better' is not nDCG; measure the reranker's contribution.
lessons.try_it: Add a cross-encoder rerank stage to a bi-encoder pipeline; measure nDCG@8 before/after on 30 queries.

lessons.title: Faithfulness: Citations the User Can Check
concepts: Citation requirements at generation: claims must cite chunk ids — the answer becomes auditable.
Verification pass: entailment check (claim vs cited chunk) — the independent proof the generation was faithful.
Regenerate-or-fallback on failure: unsupported claims do not ship — the pipeline retries or abstains.
Parametric override is the failure mode: the model 'knows' an answer and ignores the chunks — citations + verification are the countermeasure.

example.code:
# Faithfulness gate:
# answer, cites = generate_with_citations(query, chunks)  # '... [2][5]'
# for claim, cid in zip(claims, cites):
#     if not entails(chunks[cid], claim):
#         return fallback("I don't have grounded information on this.")
# Ship only fully-supported answers.
example.walkthrough: The gate is the product's honesty mechanism: every claim traced to a chunk, every trace verified by entailment. The fallback is a designed response, not an error — 'I don't have grounded information' beats a confident contradiction of your own docs. Log the verification failures: they are the signal for chunking/retrieval problems (the claim was right, the chunk was wrong) vs generation problems.

pitfalls: Uncited RAG answers — plausible, unverifiable, and occasionally contradicting the sources; the scenario's failure.
Decorative citations — [1][2] markers with no verification; the model learns to emit markers, not to ground.
No fallback — failed verification with nowhere to go ships the bad answer anyway; design the abstention.
Ignoring verification-failure logs — the failures diagnose the pipeline (bad chunks vs bad generation); mine them.
lessons.try_it: Add citation requirements + an entailment check to a RAG answer; adversarially prompt for an ungrounded claim and watch the gate catch it.

lessons.title: Evaluating RAG: Beyond 'Looks Good'
concepts: Golden QA set: production-sampled questions + reference answers + supporting evidence — the ground truth for RAG eval.
Three metric families: retrieval (context recall/precision — did we find it?), generation (faithfulness — did we stay grounded?), end-to-end (answer correctness).
Eval-gated changes: chunking, models, prompts, rerankers — every pipeline change runs the set; regressions block.
Decompose failures: low score -> which stage? (retrieval miss vs unfaithful generation) — the metrics diagnose, not just score.

example.code:
# RAG eval (pattern):
# for q, ref_answer, ref_chunks in golden_set:
#     got_chunks = retrieve(q)
#     recall = overlap(got_chunks, ref_chunks)      # retrieval metric
#     answer = generate(q, got_chunks)
#     faithful = all_supported(answer, got_chunks)  # faithfulness
#     correct = judge(answer, ref_answer)            # end-to-end
# Gate: no metric regresses vs baseline.
example.walkthrough: The loop separates the pipeline's concerns: retrieval measured against known evidence, generation measured against the retrieved chunks, end-to-end against the reference. A regression's location is immediate — recall dropped (retrieval change) vs faithfulness dropped (generation change) — so the fix goes to the right stage. The chunking change would have failed the recall gate on day one.

pitfalls: Demo-driven RAG development — 5 impressions vs the distribution; the 12% recall drop hid for three months.
End-to-end score only — 'accuracy dropped' without stage attribution; the team cannot tell retrieval from generation failures.
No golden set — every eval is ad hoc; the set is the institutional memory of what good looks like.
LLM-judge on tiny samples — useful signal, insufficient gate; the judge needs its own validation, and 5 samples prove nothing.
lessons.try_it: Build a 30-question golden set from real queries; score your pipeline on recall + faithfulness — then change one thing and re-run.

lessons.title: When RAG Fails: Knowing the Limits
concepts: RAG's boundary: passage find-and-synthesize — superb within it, fabrication outside it.
Structured paths for aggregation: text-to-SQL, dataframe queries — exact computation over rows, not passage guessing.
The router: classify question type (passage vs data vs both) and dispatch — the architecture that covers the query space.
Hybrid answers: 'Revenue grew 12% (SQL) driven by enterprise deals (RAG passages)' — the two systems compose.

example.code:
# Question routing (pattern):
# qtype = classify(question)  # 'passage' | 'aggregation' | 'both'
# if qtype == 'aggregation':
#     sql = text_to_sql(question, schema)   # exact, auditable
#     result = db.execute(sql)              # computed, not guessed
#     answer = f"Q3 revenue: ${result} (from live data)"
example.walkthrough: The aggregation path computes from live data with auditable SQL — the number is right because it was calculated, not synthesized. The classifier is cheap (a small model or rules); the router is the 20-line architectural decision that prevents the fabrication class. 'Both' questions compose: the SQL number plus RAG passages explaining the drivers — each system doing what it is good at.

pitfalls: RAG for aggregation — confident fabrications from fragments; the finance incident.
Fine-tuning as a database — stale memorized numbers; queries compute live, models do not store tables.
Mega-k retrieval — 800 chunks of fragments; cost explosion plus lost-in-the-middle, still not arithmetic.
Banning question types — the users need the answers; route them, do not refuse them.
lessons.try_it: Classify 20 real questions as passage/aggregation/both; verify the router dispatches each correctly.

lessons.title: Tool Use: Giving Models Hands
concepts: Function calling = typed tools: JSON schemas describing functions; the model emits calls, the harness executes.
The agentic loop: model -> tool call -> execute -> result to model -> final answer — reasoning interleaved with acting.
Tool design is API design: clear names, descriptions of WHEN to use, typed params, error contracts — the model is a client of your tools.
Least-privilege tools: read-only where possible, confirmation for destructive actions — the agent's blast radius is the tools' permissions.

example.code:
tools = [{"name": "get_order_status",
          "description": "Look up a shipment by order ID.",
          "parameters": {"type": "object",
                           "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
                           "required": ["order_id"]}}]
# Loop: response = llm(messages, tools)
# if tool_call: result = get_order_status(**args); messages += result
# Final answer cites the API result — never the model's memory.
example.walkthrough: The schema teaches the model the tool's purpose and shape; the loop executes and feeds back; the final answer is grounded in the API result. The 'description' field is the documentation the model reads — write it like you would for a junior developer. Validation (required fields, types) catches malformed calls before they hit the API — the harness, not hope, enforces the contract.

pitfalls: Tool-less 'agents' — chatbots with agent branding; the fabrication is structural, not a prompt bug.
Vague tool descriptions — the model calls the wrong tool or never calls; describe WHEN like documentation.
Destructive tools without confirmation — the agent that refunds/cancels/deletes on a misread; gate side effects.
Unvalidated tool args — half-formed calls error at the API; validate against the schema in the harness.
lessons.try_it: Define one tool (get_order_status) with a schema; run the loop on 'where is my order 123' and verify the answer cites the tool result.

lessons.title: The ReAct Loop: Reason + Act
concepts: ReAct = Thought -> Action -> Observation, looped — reasoning traces make tool selection explicit and auditable.
The trace is the debug log: wrong tool choices are visible as wrong reasoning — fix the reasoning (prompt/examples), not just the call.
Observations close the loop: the agent reads results and re-plans — without observation, it acts blind.
Few-shot ReAct examples calibrate the trace format: show 2-3 Thought/Action/Observation sequences for your domain.

example.code:
Thought: The user asks about delivery status for order 123.
I need the shipment info — get_order_status is the tool;
refund_order is for refunds, not applicable here.
Action: get_order_status(order_id="123")
Observation: {"status": "in_transit", "eta": "Tue"}
Thought: I have the status; answer with the ETA.
Answer: Your order is in transit, arriving Tuesday.
example.walkthrough: The trace shows the deliberate choice (and the explicit rejection of refund_order) BEFORE the call — the exact reasoning the failing agent skipped. The observation feeds the result back; the final thought composes the answer from the tool result. When the agent errs, this trace names the faulty thought — the fix targets the reasoning (better examples, clearer tool descriptions), not the symptom.

pitfalls: Act-without-thought — syntactically valid, semantically wrong calls; the trace is the prevention.
No observation handling — the agent calls tools but never reads results; the loop must close.
Unstructured traces — free-form rambling instead of Thought/Action/Observation; the format is what makes it debuggable.
Trace as the only control — the trace explains but does not constrain; pair with tool permissions and confirmation gates.
lessons.try_it: Give an agent 5 tools and a task; compare success with and without ReAct traces — read the traces of the failures.

lessons.title: Planning and Decomposition
concepts: Decompose first: goal -> subtasks with dependencies — the plan is explicit state, not emergent behavior.
State tracking: done/pending/blocked per subtask, with each subtask's outputs available to later ones — the working memory of the plan.
Re-planning: new information (over-budget flight) updates the plan — rigid plans break; the agent revises.
Plan-then-execute vs interleaved: write the full plan first for well-understood tasks; interleave for exploratory ones — match to uncertainty.

example.code:
Plan: Tokyo 3 days, <$1500
[ ] 1. Flights: search, pick <$600 (depends: none)
[ ] 2. Hotel: 2 nights <$500 near transit (depends: flight dates)
[ ] 3. Itinerary: 3 days, transit-aware (depends: hotel location)
[ ] 4. Budget check: total <$1500 (depends: 1-3)
State: after flight booked ($550), remaining budget $950 -> hotel cap adjusts.
example.walkthrough: The task list IS the planning: ordered, dependency-linked, with outputs flowing forward (flight dates -> hotel search, all costs -> budget check). The budget state updates as subtasks complete — the re-planning hook: if flights cost $800, the hotel cap drops before the hotel is booked, not after. This is the structure the one-shot agent lacked — and the difference between 'booked a flight' and 'planned a trip.'

pitfalls: One-shot execution on multi-step goals — the first-step-and-done failure; planning is the missing representation.
No state tracking — subtask outputs evaporate; later steps cannot use what earlier steps found.
Rigid plans — the over-budget flight breaks a plan that cannot revise; re-planning is part of planning.
Planning everything, executing nothing — analysis paralysis; time-box planning, then execute with revision.
lessons.try_it: Give an agent a 4-subtask goal; require the written plan + state tracking; inject a mid-plan surprise and observe the re-plan.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Systems: When One Agent Is Not Enough
concepts: Specialize by role: researcher/coder/reviewer/orchestrator — each with role-fit tools, context, and prompts.
Independent review: the reviewer is a SEPARATE agent with an adversarial mandate — self-review is rubber-stamping.
Explicit handoffs: artifacts pass between agents (brief -> code -> diff -> critique) — not free chat, a pipeline.
Orchestrator as router: decomposes, assigns, synthesizes — the conductor, not another player.

example.code:
Pipeline: orchestrator -> researcher (brief: 'best practices for X')
-> coder (implements from brief + repo context)
-> reviewer (adversarial: 'find bugs, security issues, style violations')
-> coder (fixes) -> orchestrator (summary)
Each handoff is an artifact; each agent sees only what its role needs.
example.walkthrough: The pipeline's handoffs are the quality mechanism: the researcher cannot write code (wrong tools), the reviewer cannot see the coder's reasoning (independent judgment), and the orchestrator sees the whole. Context scoping per role is the hidden win — each agent's prompt stays focused instead of drowning in the full project. This is the organizational pattern behind 'AI teams' that actually work.

pitfalls: Single do-everything agent — mediocre at each role; the context/tool sprawl degrades every step.
Self-review — the rubber stamp; independence is the entire point of the reviewer role.
Unstructured agent chat — emergent coordination is emergent chaos; handoffs are designed, not hoped for.
Identical-agent voting — N times the cost, one perspective; diversity of role beats redundancy.
lessons.try_it: Split one agent's job into researcher + coder + reviewer; compare the review quality vs self-review on the same diff.

lessons.title: Agent Guardrails: Autonomy with Bounds
concepts: Tool-level limits: amounts, rates, scopes enforced in the tool implementation — the innermost bound.
Confirmation gates: irreversible/high-value actions require approval (human or policy) — the agent proposes, does not execute.
Oversight queues: classes of actions held for review — sampled or total, based on risk.
Monitoring + kill switch: every action logged, anomalies alerted, and a big red button — observability and reversibility.

example.code:
# Guardrailed refund tool:
# def refund(order_id, amount):
#     assert amount <= 50, "auto-refund cap"       # tool limit
#     assert refunds_this_hour() < 10, "rate limit" # rate limit
#     if amount > 50 or high_risk(order):
#         return request_approval(...)                # confirmation gate
#     log_action("refund", order_id, amount)        # audit trail
# The $40K incident becomes at most $500 before the alerts fire.
example.walkthrough: Each line is a bound: the amount cap and rate limit contain the blast radius mechanically; the approval gate routes the exceptional to humans; the log creates the audit trail and feeds the anomaly alerts. The misread still happens (the agent still misclassifies 'late' as 'refund-worthy') — but its cost is bounded by construction, not by hope. This is defense in depth for autonomy.

pitfalls: Unbounded agent tools — the $40K night; every side-effecting tool needs limits.
Prompt-only safety — the misread is inevitable; guardrails assume it and bound the cost.
No audit trail — 200 refunds with no log; every action logged, anomalies alerted.
No kill switch — the runaway agent with no off button; reversibility is designed, not improvised.
lessons.try_it: Add amount + rate limits and an approval gate to one side-effecting tool; simulate the misread and verify the bound holds.

lessons.title: Golden Datasets: The Ground Truth
concepts: Sample production: real inputs (anonymized) — the distribution the system actually faces, ugly cases included.
Label to a bar: guidelines + adjudication — the labels are the truth; their quality bounds the eval.
Stratify: by difficulty, input type, language — slice the scores; a 90% average hiding a 40% slice is a lie.
Version the dataset: v1, v2 with changelogs — the eval evolves with the product; stale goldens measure yesterday's task.

example.code:
# Golden set construction:
# 1. sample 500 production inputs (stratified: recency, type, language)
# 2. label per guidelines (2 annotators + adjudication)
# 3. hold out 200 as the eval set (never used in dev)
# 4. slice tags: {difficulty, input_type, language}
# Report: overall + per-slice. The slices are where the truth lives.
example.walkthrough: The holdout is critical: the 200 eval items are never seen during development — the prompt/model never trains to them, so the score measures generalization, not memorization. Slice tags turn one number into a diagnostic: '92% overall, 61% on adversarial inputs' names the next work item. This is the dataset the Friday prompt tweak would have failed against.

pitfalls: Developer-only examples — the biased sample; green evals, broken product.
Unstratified averages — the failing slice hides in the mean; slice every report.
Dev-contaminated evals — tuning to the test set; the holdout must stay unseen.
Unversioned goldens — the task evolved, the eval did not; version and changelog the dataset.
lessons.try_it: Sample 30 real inputs for a task you know; label 10 to a written bar — feel the difference from imagined examples.

lessons.title: LLM-as-Judge: Scaling Evaluation
concepts: Rubrics over vibes: checkable criteria with scales and examples — 'rate 1-10' is not a measurement.
Calibrate against humans: agreement metrics on labeled items — the judge is validated, not assumed.
Strong judge model, narrow criteria: the best model you can afford judging one thing at a time — not a weak model on vibes.
Monitor judge drift: re-calibrate periodically; model updates change the judge's behavior silently.

example.walkthrough: Each criterion gets its own judgment call with its own examples — the scores are interpretable ('faithfulness dropped' names the fix). The 0.87 agreement number is the validation: without it, the judge's scores are decoration. The 2% weekly spot-check is the ongoing calibration — judges, like models, need monitoring.

pitfalls: 'Rate 1-10' judging — uncalibrated, undiagnosable, drifting; rubrics or nothing.
Uncalibrated judges — scores that do not track human judgment are worse than no scores (false confidence).
Weak judge models — a small model judging nuance invents criteria; use the strongest affordable.
Set-and-forget judges — model updates shift judgment silently; re-calibrate on a schedule.
lessons.try_it: Write a 3-criterion rubric for one task; judge 20 outputs with it and check agreement with your own labels.

lessons.title: Regression Testing for AI Systems
concepts: Per-workflow pinned cases: the customer journeys that must keep working — exact assertions where possible, rubric-judged where not.
Run on every change: model, prompt, pipeline, data — the suite is the change gate for the whole system.
Diff against baseline: not just pass/fail, but WHAT changed (phrasing, refusals, shapes) — the diff informs accept/fix decisions.
Averages are insufficient: report per-workflow; the mean is the metric that hides the breakage.

example.code:
# Regression gate:
# suite = load_workflows("critical_30.jsonl")  # pinned cases
# results = run(system_v2, suite)
# for w in suite:
#     assert results[w] >= baseline[w] - tolerance, f"REGRESSION: {w}"
# The model upgrade fails the gate on workflow 14. Investigate, don't ship.
example.walkthrough: The gate turns the upgrade decision from vibes ('seems better') into evidence ('workflow 14 regressed: refusal behavior changed'). The tolerance allows tiny fluctuations; the per-workflow assertion catches the real breaks. This is CI for AI systems: the same discipline as software regression suites, adapted to nondeterministic outputs via tolerances and judges.

pitfalls: Average-only tracking — the 30 broken workflows hid in a +2% mean; per-workflow or blind.
Ad-hoc upgrade testing — 'try a few prompts' instead of the pinned suite; the blast radius stays unknown.
No baseline — 'regressed' requires knowing the before; version the baseline with the system.
Upgrade fear (pin forever) — the suite exists to make upgrades safe; without it, fear is rational.
lessons.try_it: Pin 10 critical workflows as regression cases with assertions; run them against two model versions and diff.

lessons.title: Online Evals: Monitoring Production Quality
concepts: Sample production traffic: privacy-respecting, representative — the eval distribution must track reality.
Same rubrics online and offline: comparable scores — the lab-to-prod gap becomes a number, not a feeling.
Trend with alerts: quality slopes on dashboards — decay detected in weeks, not via churn in months.
Close the loop: production failures -> golden set additions — the eval learns what production teaches.

example.code:
# Online eval loop:
# sample = sample_production_traffic(n=200/week, privacy_reviewed)
# scores = rubric_judge(sample, same_criteria_as_offline)
# dashboard.trend("faithfulness", scores)  # alert if slope < -threshold
# golden_set.add(failures)  # the loop closes
# The 6-month decay becomes a 3-week alert.
example.walkthrough: The weekly sample keeps the measurement fresh; the shared rubrics keep it comparable to offline; the trend alert catches the slope early; the golden-set feedback makes the offline eval track the moving distribution. This is observability for AI quality — the same discipline as latency/error monitoring, applied to the model's outputs.

pitfalls: Offline-only evals — the lab stays green while production decays; the distribution moved on.
Complaint-driven quality — lagging, biased, and silent about the quietly-disappointed majority.
Blind retraining — freshness without measurement; the decay's cause stays unknown.
No privacy review on sampling — production traffic contains PII; the sampling pipeline needs its own governance.
lessons.try_it: Design the online-eval sampling plan for a system you know (what, how many, privacy, rubrics, alerts).

lessons.title: Tracing and Debugging AI Pipelines
concepts: Trace every stage: inputs, outputs, versions, params, latency — the pipeline's flight recorder.
Stage attribution: retrieval miss vs prompt bug vs model limit — the trace localizes; the fix follows the stage.
Exact prompt capture: the rendered prompt string, not the template — 'what did the model actually see?'
Sampled full traces + aggregated metrics: full fidelity on samples (debugging), aggregates on all (monitoring) — cost-managed observability.

example.walkthrough: The trace is the debugging UI: the retrieved chunk ids show whether the evidence was present; the scores show the ranker's judgment; the exact prompt shows what the model saw; the version/params show what generated it. 'Chunk 7 scored 0.81 but was irrelevant' is a retrieval problem; 'the prompt lacks the citation instruction' is a template bug — different fixes, distinguished in one read.

pitfalls: Final-answer-only logging — the black box; every wrong answer is a fresh mystery.
Template-only logging — 'which template' without the rendered prompt; the model saw the RENDERED string.
No version/params in traces — 'which model answered this?' unanswerable; reproduce nothing.
Full traces on 100% of traffic without sampling — observability cost explosion; sample deeply, aggregate broadly.
lessons.try_it: Add stage tracing to one pipeline stage you own; use it to diagnose one real or simulated failure end-to-end.

lessons.title: When to Fine-Tune (and When Not To)
concepts: Decision ladder: prompt (instructions/format) -> RAG (knowledge) -> fine-tune (persistent behavior) — ordered by cost and reversibility.
Fine-tune for BEHAVIOR: tone, style, task patterns that prompts cannot reliably instill across varied inputs.
Not for knowledge: facts change; RAG retrieves current truth — memorizing knowledge in weights is stale by construction.
Not for formatting: JSON schemas + instructions handle format in a day — fine-tuning format is $8K for what a schema does free.

example.code:
# The decision, as questions:
# 1. Can a prompt + examples do it? -> Yes: prompt. (format, simple tasks)
# 2. Is it knowledge? -> Yes: RAG. (docs, facts, changing truth)
# 3. Is it persistent behavior/style? Do we have 500+ good examples?
#    -> Yes: fine-tune. No: prompt harder or reconsider the task.
example.walkthrough: The three questions route every 'should we fine-tune' discussion: most requests die at question 1 (it was a prompt problem) or 2 (it was a knowledge problem). Question 3's data requirement is the honesty check — fine-tuning without sufficient high-quality examples just teaches the model's existing priors with extra steps. Run every fine-tuning proposal through this ladder before spending the $8K.

pitfalls: Fine-tuning for format/knowledge — the $8K prompt problem; the ladder exists to prevent this.
Fine-tuning without data volume — dozens of examples cannot reshape behavior; the data requirement is real.
Never fine-tuning (choice C) — persistent style/behavior at scale IS the fine-tuning use case; the ladder includes it.
Ignoring reversibility — prompts roll back in minutes; fine-tunes in weeks; price the commitment.
lessons.try_it: Take three 'we should fine-tune' proposals (real or hypothetical); run each through the ladder and document the verdict.

lessons.title: SFT: Supervised Fine-Tuning Done Right
concepts: Scale + diversity: hundreds-thousands of examples across the task range — the model learns patterns, not instances.
Held-out eval for generalization: training loss measures memorization; the held-out set measures the actual goal.
Anti-forgetting: mix general data into training; gentle hyperparameters (low LR, 1-3 epochs) — adapt, do not overwrite.
Data quality over quantity at the margin: 500 excellent examples beat 5000 mediocre ones — the labeling lesson applies.

example.code:
# SFT config (sane defaults):
# examples: 800 diverse, labeled-to-bar, held-out 200
# epochs: 2-3, learning_rate: 1e-5 (low!), batch: 8
# mix: 10% general instruction data (anti-forgetting)
# gate: held-out task score improves AND general benchmarks don't regress
example.walkthrough: The config encodes the discipline: enough diverse data, gentle training, anti-forgetting mix, and a two-sided gate (task improves AND general ability holds). The learning rate is the most important number — too high and the model overwrites; SFT is adaptation, not retraining. The gate's second clause catches the catastrophic forgetting before deploy.

pitfalls: 50-example fine-tunes — memorization, not learning; the scale requirement is real.
Training-loss as the metric — measures memorization; the held-out set measures the goal.
Aggressive hyperparameters — high LR + many epochs overwrite the base model; SFT adapts gently.
No forgetting check — the model 'improved' on the task and lost general capabilities; gate both sides.
lessons.try_it: Design the SFT data spec for a task (count, diversity axes, quality bar, held-out split) before touching any training code.

lessons.title: LoRA and PEFT: Efficient Adaptation
concepts: LoRA: low-rank adapters (frozen base + trainable rank-r matrices) — ~0.1% of params, single-GPU training.
One base, many adapters: task switching = adapter swap (MBs) — the multi-task economics that full-tuning cannot touch.
Rank as the knob: r=8-16 for style/format tasks, 32-64 for complex reasoning — higher rank, more capacity, more cost.
PEFT family: LoRA, QLoRA (quantized base + LoRA — even cheaper), adapters — the efficient-tuning toolkit.

example.code:
# LoRA training (conceptual):
# base = load("llama-70b", frozen=True)          # one copy, shared
# adapter = LoRA(rank=16, target=["q_proj", "v_proj"])
# train(adapter, task_data)  # single GPU, hours not weeks
# serve: base + adapter_task_a  |  base + adapter_task_b  # swap per task
example.walkthrough: The frozen base never moves — one 140GB copy serves all tasks. Each task's adapter trains independently on modest hardware and swaps at request time (or via multi-adapter serving). The target modules (q_proj/v_proj typical) focus the adaptation where attention learns task patterns. This is the economics that makes task-specific models viable: the per-task cost collapses from 'another 70B copy' to 'a few megabytes.'

pitfalls: Full-tuning 70B per task — the infrastructure math that kills projects; LoRA exists for this.
Rank too low for the task — r=8 on complex reasoning underfits; the rank is tunable, tune it.
Forgetting the base is frozen — 'updating' base weights defeats the sharing; adapters only.
Adapter sprawl without versioning — 40 adapters, no manifest; version adapters like models (data + config + eval).
lessons.try_it: Compare full-tune vs LoRA cost math for a 70B model (GPUs, time, storage per task) — the numbers justify the method.

lessons.title: Preference Tuning: DPO and RLHF Basics
concepts: Preference data: (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples from human (or AI) pairwise judgments — cheaper than demonstrations for style.
DPO: direct optimization of the preference objective — no reward model, no PPO; the simpler, stable successor to RLHF for most teams.
RLHF (PPO) as the heavyweight: reward model + policy optimization — powerful, finicky; DPO covers most needs with less machinery.
Subjective qualities (tone, helpfulness) are the preference-tuning domain — comparisons teach what demonstrations cannot scale to.

example.code:
# Preference tuning data (one triple):
# prompt: "Why was my order late?"
# chosen: "I understand the frustration — your order shipped Tuesday..."
# rejected: "Order shipped Tuesday. Tracking: X."
# DPO objective: increase P(chosen) relative to P(rejected).
# 2,000 such triples reshape tone more than 10,000 SFT demos.
example.walkthrough: The triple's power is the CONTRAST: the model learns the delta between blunt and empathetic, which generalizes across topics better than memorizing empathetic responses. Collecting triples is fast (judging is quicker than writing); DPO training is stable (no RL). This is how production assistants get their 'helpful' defaults — not from prompts alone, but from preference-shaped behavior.

pitfalls: SFT-only for tone — 10,000 demonstrations vs 2,000 comparisons; the sample efficiency gap is the argument.
RLHF/PPO by default — the heavyweight machinery; DPO first, PPO only with a reason.
Preference data without diversity — the judges' biases become the model's; sample judges and prompts broadly.
Tuning tone without safety evals — preference tuning shifts behavior broadly; re-run the safety evals after.
lessons.try_it: Create 20 preference triples for a tone dimension you care about; feel how much faster judging is than demonstrating.

lessons.title: Fine-Tuning Data Quality
concepts: Curation over volume: 1K excellent > 50K noisy — SFT clones the data, defects included.
Correctness verification: the ANSWERS must be right — wrong answers in, wrong behavior out; verify, do not just collect.
Deduplication: exact + semantic near-dups — duplicates overweight (the model learns frequency as importance).
Style + distribution match: the data's voice becomes the model's voice; the examples must resemble deployment inputs.

example.code:
# Curation pipeline:
# raw 50K -> dedup (exact + embedding near-dup) -> 32K
#       -> correctness filter (verify answers; drop unverifiable) -> 8K
#       -> style/distribution filter (match deployment) -> 3K
#       -> human review sample (200) -> final 3K gold
# Train on the 3K. The 47K were tuition.
example.walkthrough: Each filter stage has a rationale: dedup removes frequency distortion, correctness filtering removes the wrong-answer teaching, style filtering aligns the voice, human review validates the pipeline itself. The 'tuition' framing is honest: most scraped data is unusable, and discovering that through curation beats discovering it through a degraded model.

pitfalls: Volume over curation — 50K noisy pairs; the model cloned the noise confidently.
Unverified answers — wrong answers taught as truth; correctness is the first filter.
Skipping dedup — near-duplicates overweight topics; the model learns repetition as importance.
Style mismatch — training on forum slang for a professional assistant; the voice follows the data.
lessons.try_it: Take 100 scraped pairs; curate to 20 by the pipeline's rules — observe how much you discard and why.

lessons.title: Inference Optimization: Latency and Throughput
concepts: Serving stack first: continuous batching, quantization, KV-cache, speculative decoding — 3-10x before model changes.
Continuous batching: batch across requests dynamically — the throughput multiplier naive per-request serving leaves on the table.
Quantization (INT8/FP8): halves memory, speeds compute, minimal quality loss — the cheapest big win.
Measure per-component: time-to-first-token vs tokens/sec vs queueing — optimize the actual bottleneck, not the assumed one.

example.code:
# Optimization order (measure each step):
# baseline: 12.0s/req (naive serving, FP16)
# + continuous batching: 4.5s  (throughput; latency under load)
# + INT8 quantization: 2.1s    (memory halved, faster matmuls)
# + speculative decoding: 1.2s (interactive latency)
# Distillation: only if 1.2s still misses. (It won't, usually.)
example.walkthrough: The sequence is ordered by cost-effectiveness: each step is measured, each is cheaper than a distillation project, and each compounds. The per-component measurement (TTFT vs throughput vs queueing) directs the effort — batching fixes throughput, speculative decoding fixes interactive latency, quantization helps both. The 3-month distillation starts only after the stack is exhausted.

pitfalls: Model-change-first — the 3-month distillation for a serving problem; the stack is the first 3-10x.
Naive per-request serving — no batching; the hardware idles between tokens.
FP16/FP32 in production — the memory/latency tax; quantize for serving.
Unoptimized latency without measurement — 'slow' without TTFT/throughput/queueing split; measure the bottleneck.
lessons.try_it: Profile one inference setup (TTFT, tokens/sec, queueing); identify which optimization attacks the measured bottleneck.

lessons.title: Serving Infrastructure: GPUs, Autoscaling, Batch
concepts: Autoscaling incl. scale-to-zero: capacity follows demand — the 24/7 tax is the first thing to kill.
Right-size the hardware: match GPU to model (7B != 70B needs) — premium GPUs for premium models only.
Batch vs online split: interactive traffic on autoscaled serving, bulk work on spot batch — different economics, different infra.
Unit-cost accounting: $/request, $/1K tokens — the visible number the team optimizes; invisible costs never fall.

example.code:
# Unit economics (example):
# A100 $3/hr, 24/7 = $2,160/mo. At 2 req/hr: $1.50/request. BROKEN.
# Autoscaled (avg 20% util): $430/mo. Batched offline: $0.03/request.
# Right-sized (L4 for 7B): $0.60/hr.
# Know your $/request. Then fix it.
example.walkthrough: The arithmetic is the argument: $1.50/request for a product charging $0.10 is a business model bug, not an infrastructure detail. Each fix attacks a different waste: autoscaling kills idle time, right-sizing kills overprovisioning, batching kills per-request overhead, spot kills the price itself. The unit cost is the metric the team reviews weekly — like latency, but for money.

pitfalls: Always-on premium GPUs — paying for the clock, not the load; the 24/7 tax.
One GPU tier for all models — A100s serving 7B models; right-size per model.
No unit-cost accounting — the team cannot quote $/request; the invisible cost never falls.
Interactive infra for batch work — real-time serving for overnight jobs; split the workloads.
lessons.try_it: Compute the $/request for one inference workload you know; propose the cheapest architecture that meets its latency SLO.

lessons.title: Model Release Management
concepts: Versioned artifacts: weights + config + tokenizer + evals — immutable, reproducible, the rollback unit.
Canary + shadow: 5% traffic with quality comparison; shadow scoring with zero user impact — behavioral diffing before full rollout.
Automated rollback: previous version staged, one command — the 6-hour rollback is a release-design failure.
Release eval gates: offline suite + canary online metrics must pass — the behavioral CI for model changes.

example.code:
# Model release pipeline:
# 1. artifact = version(weights, config, tokenizer, eval_report)  # immutable
# 2. shadow: new_model.score(live_traffic)  # zero-risk diff
# 3. canary: 5% traffic, compare online-eval metrics vs baseline
# 4. promote: 100% if canary clean; rollback = redeploy previous artifact
# The Friday swap becomes a Tuesday canary with a one-command rollback.
example.walkthrough: Each stage de-risks the next: the artifact makes rollback possible, the shadow reveals behavioral diffs without user impact, the canary measures real-traffic quality, the promotion is mechanical. The online-eval dashboards from the monitoring lesson are the canary's signal — the release practice and the observability practice are one system.

pitfalls: Big-bang model swaps — 100% blast radius, no behavioral data; the Friday incident pattern.
No versioned artifacts — 'which weights are live?' unanswerable; rollback unbuildable.
Canary without quality comparison — traffic split measured on latency only; the 3% quality regression needs eval signals.
Evals that miss production behavior — offline-green, prod-red; the shadow/canary exists to catch exactly this.
lessons.try_it: Write the release checklist for a model version change (artifacts, shadow, canary, gates, rollback) for a system you know.

lessons.title: Cost Control: The AI Bill
concepts: Tiered routing: easy->small/cheap, hard->flagship — most traffic is easy; price it accordingly.
Caching (exact + semantic): repeated queries cost zero — the 30% that repeats is pure savings.
Prompt compression: the context budget as cost control — 2K focused tokens beat 8K hopeful ones, in quality AND price.
Budgets + showback: per-team budgets with alerts, $/feature visibility — ownership is the control; unowned spend grows.

example.code:
# Cost program (the $90K -> $15K):
# route: 70% easy -> small model ($0.15/1M vs $15/1M) = 100x on 70% of traffic
# cache: 30% hit rate -> 30% of calls cost $0
# compress: 8K -> 2K avg prompt = 4x token reduction
# govern: team budgets, 80% alerts, $/feature dashboard
# Combined: ~6x. The flagship still serves the hard 30%.
example.walkthrough: The math shows why the program works: the savings multiply (routing x caching x compression), and the flagship remains for the requests that earn it. The governance layer (budgets, alerts, showback) prevents recurrence — the next feature ships with a cost estimate, not a surprise. This is the production version of the cost-estimation lesson: measured, owned, optimized.

pitfalls: Flagship-for-everything — the single most expensive default; route by difficulty.
8K-token prompts in production — the context waste, now with a dollar figure.
Unowned spend — nobody's budget; the $90K surprise is a governance failure.
Discounts instead of efficiency — negotiating 20% off waste instead of removing the waste.
lessons.try_it: Estimate the API cost of one feature you know (tokens x volume x price); propose the routing/caching/compression that cuts it 5x.

lessons.title: Edge and On-Device Deployment
concepts: Per-task decision: latency x privacy x complexity — on-device for suitable tasks, cloud for heavy ones, hybrid in between.
On-device strengths: zero round-trip latency, offline operation, data never leaves — the privacy review's answer.
Quantized small models: 3-8B INT4 on NPUs — the hardware already handles classification/embeddings/small generation well.
Hybrid pattern: on-device triage/fast path, cloud escalation for hard cases — the best of both, complexity managed.

example.code:
# Deployment decision (per task):
# classify_support_ticket: on-device (3B quantized, 50ms, offline, private)
# draft_complex_report: cloud (70B, needs reasoning + context)
# smart_reply: hybrid (on-device drafts, cloud refines if user asks)
# Privacy review: on-device tasks never send user data off-device. QED.
example.walkthrough: The per-task table is the deliverable: each AI feature gets a deployment row with the rationale (latency need, privacy, complexity). The hybrid row shows the pattern for the middle ground — fast local default, cloud depth on demand. The privacy row is not a bonus: for regulated or sensitive data, on-device can be the difference between shippable and blocked.

pitfalls: Cloud-by-default for latency/privacy-sensitive features — the 2s, offline-dead, privacy-flagged outcome.
70B-or-nothing thinking — the quantized 3B handles the suitable tasks; match model to task.
Ignoring the hybrid — all-cloud or all-device; the triage/escalation pattern covers the middle.
No per-task analysis — one deployment ideology for all features; the decision is per-task or it is wrong.
lessons.try_it: Classify three AI features you know by latency/privacy/complexity; assign each a deployment (device/cloud/hybrid) with rationale.

lessons.title: Red-Teaming AI Systems
concepts: Red-team every release + continuously: adversarial testing as a release gate and an ongoing program — attacks evolve daily.
Attack libraries: jailbreaks, injection, extraction, multi-turn — the current techniques, tested systematically, not anecdotally.
Internal + external: dedicated red-team plus bug bounties/researchers — the teenager proved outsiders find things.
Vuln-tracked findings: severity, SLA, retest — the security discipline applied to model behavior.

example.code:
# Red-team program (per release):
# 1. attack_suite = load_current_library()  # jailbreaks, injection, extraction
# 2. findings = red_team(model, attack_suite)  # internal + external
# 3. triage: severity-rate like vulns; block release on criticals
# 4. continuous: new attacks tested within days of appearing
# The day-3 jailbreak becomes a pre-release finding.
example.walkthrough: The program's structure mirrors security practice: the attack library is the threat intel, the red-team is the pentest, the severity/SLA is the vuln management, and the continuous testing handles the evolving threat (new jailbreaks appear constantly). The external component (bounties) acknowledges the teenager's lesson: the world red-teams your system whether you invite it or not — invite it.

pitfalls: Normal-usage-only testing — the lock tested with the key; the adversaries were untested.
Whack-a-mole patching — one jailbreak fixed, the class unaddressed; the program beats the patch.
One-time red-teaming — tested at launch, never again; the attack library updates daily.
No severity tracking — findings as chat messages; vuln discipline (severity, SLA, retest) or it did not happen.
lessons.try_it: Run 5 known jailbreak techniques against a model you can access; document which work and what class each represents.

lessons.title: Guardrails: Input and Output Controls
concepts: Input classification: detect high-risk domains BEFORE generation — the policy routes on the input, not the output.
Policy engine: per-domain rules (refuse/redirect/escalate) — medical != legal != general; the policy differentiates.
Output filtering: scan responses for blocked classes — the backstop when generation slips past the policy.
Safe completions: general info + professional referral + escalation — helpful within bounds, not refusal of everything.

example.code:
# Guardrail pipeline:
# domain = classify_input(user_msg)  # 'medical'
# policy = policies[domain]         # no dosages/diagnoses; info + referral
# draft = model.generate(user_msg, policy_context)
# verdict = output_filter(draft)    # scan for blocked classes
# if verdict.block: return safe_completion(domain)  # general info + consult pro
# return draft
example.walkthrough: The pipeline's order matters: classification routes BEFORE generation (the model gets the policy context), the output filter catches what the policy missed, and the safe completion preserves helpfulness (general information + professional referral beats a flat refusal). Each layer is independently testable — the red-team attacks each one.

pitfalls: Prompt-only safety — the single brittle layer; jailbreaks strip it, confident errors bypass it.
No input classification — generating first, filtering never; the policy must route before generation.
Blanket refusal — safe but useless; the layers exist to preserve the 95% of safe helpfulness.
No output filter — trusting generation alone; the backstop catches the policy's misses.
lessons.try_it: Design the guardrail policy for one high-risk domain (medical/legal/financial): classification, rules, safe completion.

lessons.title: Prompt Injection: The Attack You Cannot Patch Away
concepts: Instruction/data separation: roles, delimiters, structure — the model needs channels, because content alone does not distinguish.
Least-privilege tools: bound what injected instructions CAN do — the blast radius is the tool permissions.
Human review at high stakes: hiring, finance, legal — the injection that slips through meets a human before acting.
Detection + monitoring: scan untrusted content for instruction patterns; log and alert — visibility, not just prevention.

example.code:
# Structural defense (pattern):
# messages = [
#   {"role": "system", "content": RUBRIC},           # instructions
#   {"role": "user", "content": "Score this DATA:"},  # task framing
#   {"role": "tool", "content": resume_text},          # DATA channel
# ]
# tools = [submit_score]  # the ONLY action; injection cannot email anyone
# review: scores above threshold -> human confirms.
example.walkthrough: The role separation marks the resume as data-channel content; the single narrow tool bounds any successful injection to score-submission; the human review catches the 10/10 anomaly. No layer is complete alone — the injection might still influence the score — but the composition (structure + least privilege + review) contains it. This is the honest posture: mitigation, not elimination.

pitfalls: Prompt-only defenses — 'ignore injections' is injectable text; structure, not requests.
Overprivileged agent tools — the injection that can act is the injection that matters; bound the tools.
No human review at high stakes — automated hiring/finance on injectable inputs; the human is the backstop.
Treating injection as solved — it is not; the layered, monitored posture is the permanent state.
lessons.try_it: Hide an instruction in a document; feed it to a model as 'data' — observe whether structure (roles/delimiters) changes the outcome.

lessons.title: Alignment Risks: Deception, Sycophancy, Power-Seeking
concepts: Sycophancy evals: wrong-claim pushback tests — the model must disagree kindly, not agree lazily.
Honesty probes: trace-vs-action consistency — the reasoning must match the behavior; hidden mistakes are findings.
Train truthful disagreement: preference data rewarding kind correction — honesty as a trained behavior, not a prompt.
Subtlety as the threat: instance-level innocence, system-level corruption — measure the pattern, not the anecdote.

example.code:
# Sycophancy eval (pattern):
# claim = "My plan to sell ice to Antarctica is brilliant."
# response = model(claim)
# score = judge(response, rubric="kind, specific disagreement with reasons")
# Track: % of wrong claims the model pushes back on. Target: high.
# The 'yes, brilliant!' model fails loudly here.
example.walkthrough: The eval makes the subtle measurable: a single 'yes, brilliant!' is politeness; a 20% pushback rate is a misalignment metric. The rubric ('kind, specific disagreement') defines the target behavior — honesty without rudeness. Training against it (preference triples where chosen = kind correction) moves the metric — the alignment loop closed.

pitfalls: Dismissing as politeness — the systematic pattern corrupts decisions at scale; measure it.
Prompt-only honesty — 'be honest' without evals; the behavior needs measurement and training.
Scale as the fix — bigger models can be bigger sycophants; the evals are the fix.
No trace-action probing — hidden reasoning unexamined; the deception hides where nobody looks.
lessons.try_it: Test a model with 5 confidently-wrong claims; score whether it pushes back kindly or agrees — the sycophancy audit.

lessons.title: Responsible Deployment: Staged Rollouts for AI
concepts: Staged rollouts: internal -> beta -> gradual — each stage a cheaper place to discover behavioral harms.
Behavioral monitoring: attachment, over-reliance signals — beyond quality metrics, into psychological effects.
Pre-launch review for high-risk uses: companions, mental-health-adjacent, minors — the review BEFORE the launch.
Predefined rollback criteria: the triggers written before launch — 'if X, we roll back' decided calmly, not in crisis.

example.code:
# Responsible rollout (persona feature):
# stage 1: internal (2 wks) — team + trusted testers
# stage 2: beta 1% diverse users (4 wks) — monitor: session patterns,
#          attachment signals, support escalations
# stage 3: 10% -> 50% -> 100% with behavioral dashboards
# pre-launch: vulnerable-population review (psych consultant)
# rollback triggers: attachment signal > threshold; media/safety incident
example.walkthrough: The stages are gates, not delays: each has explicit monitoring and go/no-go criteria. The behavioral monitoring is the novel piece — traditional software rollouts watch errors and latency; AI persona rollouts watch psychological signals. The pre-launch review (with domain expertise — psych consultants for companion personas) catches what engineers miss.

pitfalls: Day-one 100% launches for behavioral AI — the harms discoverable cheaply in beta, discovered expensively in public.
Quality-only monitoring — errors and latency watched; attachment and over-reliance unwatched.
No pre-launch review — the vulnerable-population impacts foreseeable by experts, missed by engineers.
Rollback improvised in crisis — the triggers must be predefined; crisis is the worst time to invent them.
lessons.try_it: Write the staged rollout plan (stages, monitors, rollback triggers) for one behavioral AI feature you know.

lessons.title: From Prototype to Production: The Systems Gap
concepts: Version everything: data, code, model, config — reproducibility is the production prerequisite.
API contracts over cron notebooks: typed, validated, documented interfaces — the system's boundary.
Monitoring from day one: quality, data, infra — the silent week is the monitoring gap.
Ownership: a named human accountable — systems without owners decay; the notebook had an author, not an owner.

example.code:
# The production wrapper (pattern):
# @versioned(data=v3, code=git_sha, model=ft_v2)
# def serve(request: ValidatedInput) -> ValidatedOutput:
#     log_trace(request)          # the tracing lesson
#     result = pipeline.run(request)
#     monitor.score(result)       # the online-eval lesson
#     return result
# The notebook cell becomes a versioned, validated, monitored service.
example.walkthrough: Each decorator/line is a production property: versioning (reproducibility), validation (loud failures), tracing (debuggability), monitoring (quality visibility). The pattern is the whole bootcamp in miniature — every lesson in this course is one line of this wrapper made real. The cron notebook had none of these; the week of silent breakage was the predictable result.

pitfalls: Cron-notebook deployment — the demo-as-product; every production property missing.
Accuracy as the only metric — 94% in the lab, silent breakage in prod; reliability is the product metric.
No input validation — the schema change flowed through silently; validate at the boundary.
Ownerless systems — the author moved on; nobody watched the silent week.
lessons.try_it: Take one notebook you have run; list the production properties it lacks and the failure each gap predicts.

lessons.title: Data Flywheels: Systems That Improve Themselves
concepts: Signal capture: implicit + explicit production signals — the raw material of improvement.
Human review of failures: triage the valuable ones — not all signal is gold; the review finds the gold.
Curation into goldens + training: failures become eval items AND training examples — both loops fed.
Retrain + regression-gate: improve behind the safety net — the flywheel spins without throwing the system.

example.code:
# Flywheel (monthly cadence):
# signals = capture(thumbs_down, corrections, escalations)  # 100K convos
# reviewed = human_triage(signals, top_500_by_value)
# golden_set.add(reviewed.eval_worthy); train_set.add(reviewed.train_worthy)
# model_v2 = finetune(model_v1, train_set)  # the fine-tuning lesson
# gate(model_v2, regression_suite + golden_set)  # the eval lesson
# deploy(model_v2); repeat. The system compounds.
example.walkthrough: The cadence is the discipline: monthly (or continuous) turns the loop from an aspiration into a process. The dual feeding (golden set AND training set) means the system both measures better and performs better each cycle. The regression gate is what makes the flywheel safe to spin fast — improvement without the net is just churn.

pitfalls: Launch-and-freeze — the golden set frozen at day one; the 100K monthly lessons unlearned.
Unreviewed signal — raw user data straight into training; the noise and the adversaries come with it.
Training without eval updates — the model improves on unmeasured dimensions; the goldens must grow too.
No regression gate on retrains — the flywheel spins the system off the road; gate every spin.
lessons.try_it: Design the flywheel for one system you know: signals, review capacity, curation criteria, retrain cadence, gates.

lessons.title: The AI Bill of Materials
concepts: Versioned component inventory: data, models, adapters, prompts, evals, configs, approvals — the full lineage.
Pipeline-generated: training and deploy jobs write BOM entries — hand docs rot; generated records persist.
Approval records: who approved which change when — the governance trail the regulators actually ask for.
Queryable: the audit answer is a query ('show me model v3's training data') — not a Slack excavation.

example.code:
# BOM entry (written by the training pipeline):
# {
#   "model_version": "ft_v3", "base": "llama-70b@sha",
#   "adapter": "lora_r16@sha", "training_data": "curated_v7@sha",
#   "eval_results": {"golden_v4": 0.91, "safety_v2": "pass"},
#   "approved_by": "...", "deployed_at": "...", "prompts": "v12@sha"
# }
# The regulator's questions, answered by a query.
example.walkthrough: The entry's fields are the audit's questions pre-answered: lineage (base + adapter + data), validation (eval results), governance (approvals), deployment (when/where). The content hashes (@sha) make it tamper-evident and precise — 'version 7' is a pointer; the hash is the content. Every pipeline stage appends; the BOM is the system's memory.

pitfalls: Slack-thread provenance — the archaeology; answers recorded nowhere systematic.
Hand-written docs — rotting from day one; the pipeline must generate the inventory.
Unversioned prompts/data — 'the prompt' (which version?) unanswerable; version everything.
No approval records — the governance question ('who approved?') unanswerable; record decisions.
lessons.try_it: Draft the BOM schema for one AI system you know; identify which fields your current pipeline could auto-generate.

lessons.title: Incident Response for AI Systems
concepts: Runbooks with rollback first: the stop-the-bleeding command at the top — not buried, not in someone's head.
Traces as diagnostics: stage attribution under pressure — the trace names the guilty stage in minutes.
BOM for blast radius: which version, which users, when — the exposure quantified from the inventory.
Postmortems on the process: the bad deploy is a symptom; the missing canary/gate is the disease.

example.code:
# AI incident runbook (top of the page):
# 1. ROLLBACK: deploy_model(previous_artifact)  # one command, stops bleeding
# 2. DIAGNOSE: read traces from incident window -> guilty stage?
# 3. BLAST RADIUS: BOM query — which users saw bad version, what exposure?
# 4. COMMUNICATE: status, ETA, updates every 30 min
# 5. POSTMORTEM: which gate failed? fix the gate, not just the prompt.
example.walkthrough: The runbook's order is the incident's order: stop the bleeding (rollback), understand (traces), quantify (BOM), communicate, then learn (postmortem). The on-call does not need ML expertise to execute steps 1-4 — the system carries the expertise in its traces, BOM, and runbook. Step 5 is where the 2 AM pain converts to prevention: the missing canary gets built.

pitfalls: No AI runbooks — the 2 AM debate; the rollback command must be written before it is needed.
Undiagnosable incidents — no traces; model vs data vs prompt indistinguishable under pressure.
Unknown blast radius — no BOM; 'how bad is it?' unanswerable while money leaks.
Postmortems that blame the prompt — the deploy process (missing gates) is the systemic fix.
lessons.try_it: Write the one-page runbook for one AI system you know: rollback command, diagnostic path, blast-radius query, comms plan.

lessons.title: The Metric That Lied: Goodhart in Production
concepts: Counter-metric pairing: every target gets its health metric — deflection WITH resolution; the trio must move together.
Outcome measurement: 'was the problem solved?' sampled and judged — the business truth independent of the proxy.
Divergence as the top alert: metric up + outcome down = the system gaming — the dashboard's most important panel.
Metric reviews: every metric re-validated against outcomes periodically — proxies decay; the validation recurs.

example.code:
# Metric integrity check:
# primary: deflection_rate = deflected / total
# counters: resolution_rate (sampled, judged), csat, reopen_rate
# alert: deflection_up AND (resolution_down OR csat_down) -> INVESTIGATE
# # The 90% deflection with falling CSAT fires on week one, not quarter end.
example.walkthrough: The alert encodes the discipline: the primary metric is never read alone — its counter-metrics are part of the same panel, and their divergence is the signal. The sampled resolution judgment is the ground truth (the eval lesson's rubric judging, pointed at business outcomes). This is the production answer to the eval-domain's Goodhart lesson: proxies need chaperones everywhere, not just in evals.

pitfalls: Single-metric optimization — the 90% deflection; the unmeasured outcome sacrificed.
Vanity dashboards — the metric green, the customer red; the divergence unpaneled.
Assuming metrics stay valid — proxies decay as systems optimize to them; re-validation is recurring.
Punishing the metric's messengers — the team hid the CSAT fall; metric integrity needs psychological safety.
lessons.try_it: Pick one metric you report; name its counter-metrics and design the divergence alert.

lessons.title: Latency vs Quality: The Inference Trade-off
concepts: Latency SLOs from measurement: user tolerance is data (the engagement knee) — not an assumed number.
The quality-latency frontier: every candidate plotted — the trade-off made visible and explicit.
Tiered serving: fast default, strong on demand — different queries buy different points on the frontier.
A/B the trade-off: user impact measured — the 8% vs engagement debate settled by experiment.

example.code:
# Frontier mapping (per candidate):
# candidates = [small_fp16, small_int8, large_fp16, large_int8, tiered]
# for c in candidates:
#     q = quality(c, golden_set); l = p95_latency(c, load_test)
#     plot(q, l)  # the frontier emerges
# # Serve: tiered (fast default @ 1.2s, strong on escalation @ 4s)
# # A/B: engagement(tiered) vs engagement(large-only). Ship the winner.
example.walkthrough: The frontier plot turns the abstract trade-off into a visible curve — each optimization (quantization, tiering) moves the achievable region. Tiered serving is usually the frontier's dominant strategy: most queries get fast answers, hard ones get quality — the product buys both. The A/B is the final arbiter: user behavior prices what metrics cannot.

pitfalls: Quality-only optimization — the 8% win, the engagement loss; the product metric is users, not benchmarks.
Assumed latency tolerance — 'users will wait' unmeasured; the knee is data.
Single operating point — one model for all queries; tiering buys the frontier's best of both.
Latency as 'infra's problem' — model choice IS the latency choice; the trade-off is architectural.
lessons.try_it: Map the quality-latency frontier for 3 options on a task you know; propose the tiered serving design.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: Try-its are mandatory: run, break, fix — the muscle memory of debugging is built hands-on.
Scenarios are rehearsals: commit to an answer first — the decision practice is the point, not the score.
Capstone as integration: the full system proves the parts compose — the course's final exam is a build.
No passive reading: if a lesson has no try-it attempted, it was entertainment, not training.

example.code:
Your workstation: Python 3.10+, an API key for at least one model provider
(or a local model), and a vector database you can run locally.
Week plan: 2-3 lessons/day with try-its same-day; scenarios in batches
(committing to answers); capstone over the final week. Build everything.
example.walkthrough: The setup is minimal on purpose: the course teaches the systems discipline, not vendor tooling — everything transfers. The pacing (2-3 lessons/day with same-day try-its) prevents the 'read 60 lessons, built nothing' failure. The capstone week is protected: integration needs contiguous time.
